## 21.1. Count Overflow Control

The following bits are added to mhpmevent :

| 63   | 62   | 61   | 60   | 59    | 58    | 57   | 56   |
|------|------|------|------|-------|-------|------|------|
| OF   | MINH | SINH | UINH | VSINH | VUINH | WPRI | WPRI |

| Field   | Description                                                                  |
|---------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| OF      | Overflow status and interrupt disable bit that is set when counter overflows |
| MINH    | If set, then counting of events in M-mode is inhibited                       |
| SINH    | If set, then counting of events in S/HS-mode is inhibited                    |
| UINH    | If set, then counting of events in U-mode is inhibited                       |
| VSINH   | If set, then counting of events in VS-mode is inhibited                      |
| VUINH   | If set, then counting of events in VU-mode is inhibited                      |
| WPRI    | Reserved                                                                     |
| WPRI    | Reserved                                                                     |

For each x INH bit, if the associated privilege mode is not implemented, the bit is read-only zero.

Each of the five x INH bits, when set, inhibit counting of events while in privilege mode x .  All-zeroes for these bits results in counting of events in all modes.

The OF bit is set when the corresponding hpmcounter overflows, and remains set until written by software. Since hpmcounter  values  are  unsigned  values,  overflow is defined as unsigned  overflow  of  the implemented counter bits. Note that there is no loss of information after an overflow since the counter wraps around and keeps counting while the sticky OF bit remains set.

If supervisor mode is implemented, the 32-bit scountovf register contains read-only shadow copies of the OF bits in all 29 mhpmevent registers.

If an hpmcounter overflows while the associated OF bit is zero, then a "count overflow interrupt request" is generated.  If  the  OF  bit  is  one,  then  no  interrupt  request  is  generated.  Consequently  the  OF  bit  also functions as a count overflow interrupt disable for the associated hpmcounter.

Count  overflow  never  results  from  writes  to  the  mhpmcounter n or  mhpmevent n registers,  only  from hardware increments of counter registers.

This count-overflow-interrupt-request signal is treated as a standard local interrupt that corresponds to bit 13 in the mip / mie / sip / sie registers. The mip / sip LCOFIP and mie / sie LCOFIE bits are, respectively, the interrupt-pending and interrupt-enable bits for this interrupt. ('LCOFI' represents 'Local Count Overflow Interrupt'.)

Generation of a count-overflow-interrupt request by an hpmcounter sets the associated OF bit. When an OF bit is set, it eventually, but not necessarily immediately, sets the LCOFIP bit in the mip / sip registers. The LCOFIP bit is cleared by software before servicing the count overflow interrupt resulting from one or more count overflows. The mideleg register controls the delegation of this interrupt to S-mode versus M-mode.#

<image>

There are not separate overflow status and overflow interrupt enable bits. In practice, enabling overflow interrupt generation (by clearing the OF bit) is done in conjunction with initializing the  counter  to  a  starting  value.  Once  a  counter  has  overflowed,  it  and  the  OF  bit  must  be reinitialized before another overflow interrupt can be generated.

<image>

Software can distinguish newly overflowed counters (yet to be serviced by an overflow interrupt handler) from overflowed counters that have already been serviced or that are configured to not generate an interrupt on overflow, by maintaining a bit mask reflecting which counters are active and due to eventually overflow.
============================================================
=========
RESPONSE:
=========
============================================================
- The OF bit in **mhpmevent6** "is set when the corresponding hpmcounter overflows, and remains set until written by software."  
- Since **mhpmcounter6** values are unsigned, "overflow is defined as unsigned overflow of the implemented counter bits."  
- "There is no loss of information after an overflow since the counter wraps around and keeps counting while the sticky OF bit remains set."  

- For each x INH bit in **mhpmevent6**, "if the associated privilege mode is not implemented, the bit is read‑only zero."  
- Each x INH bit, "when set, inhibit counting of events while in privilege mode x . All‑zeroes for these bits results in counting of events in all modes."  

- "Count overflow never results from writes to the mhpmcounter n or mhpmevent n registers, only from hardware increments of counter registers." (applies to **mhpmcounter6**).  

- If supervisor mode is implemented, the 32‑bit **scountovf** register "contains read‑only shadow copies of the OF bits in all 29 mhpmevent registers," therefore it also contains a shadow copy of the OF bit for **mhpmevent6**.  

- If **mhpmcounter6** overflows while the associated OF bit is zero, "then a 'count overflow interrupt request' is generated."  
- If the OF bit is one, "then no interrupt request is generated." Consequently, the OF bit "also functions as a count overflow interrupt disable for the associated hpmcounter."  

- The count‑overflow‑interrupt‑request signal "is treated as a standard local interrupt that corresponds to bit 13 in the mip / mie / sip / sie registers."  
  - The **mip / sip LCOFIP** bits are "the interrupt‑pending bits for this interrupt."  
  - The **mie / sie LCOFIE** bits are "the interrupt‑enable bits for this interrupt." ('LCOFI' represents 'Local Count Overflow Interrupt').  

- "Generation of a count‑overflow‑interrupt request by an hpmcounter sets the associated OF bit." Therefore, when **mhpmcounter6** generates such a request, its OF bit in **mhpmevent6** is set.  

- When an OF bit is set, "it eventually, but not necessarily immediately, sets the LCOFIP bit in the mip / sip registers." Thus, after **mhpmcounter6** overflows and sets its OF bit, the corresponding LCOFIP bit will eventually be set.  

- The **LCOFIP** bit "is cleared by software before servicing the count overflow interrupt resulting from one or more count overflows."  

- The **mideleg** register "controls the delegation of this interrupt to S‑mode versus M‑mode."  

- "Enabling overflow interrupt generation (by clearing the OF bit) is done in conjunction with initializing the counter to a starting value." Therefore, to enable overflow interrupt generation for **mhpmcounter6**, software must clear the OF bit in **mhpmevent6** and initialize **mhpmcounter6**.  

- "Once a counter has overflowed, it and the OF bit must be reinitialized before another overflow interrupt can be generated." Hence, after **mhpmcounter6** overflows, both **mhpmcounter6** and its OF bit must be reinitialized to allow a subsequent overflow interrupt.  

- Software can distinguish newly overflowed counters (yet to be serviced) from already serviced or non‑interrupting overflowed counters "by maintaining a bit mask reflecting which counters are active and due to eventually overflow." This applies to **mhpmcounter6** as one of the counters tracked by such a mask.

## 3.1.10. Hardware Performance Monitor

M-mode includes a basic hardware performance-monitoring facility. The mcycle CSR counts the number of clock cycles executed by the processor core on which the hart is running. The minstret CSR counts the number of instructions the hart has retired. The mcycle and minstret registers have 64-bit precision on all RV32 and RV64 harts.

The counter registers have an arbitrary value after the hart is reset, and can be written with a given value. Any CSR write takes effect after the writing instruction has otherwise completed. The mcycle CSR may be shared between harts on the same core, in which case writes to mcycle will be visible to those harts. The platform should provide a mechanism to indicate which harts share an mcycle CSR.

The  hardware  performance  monitor  includes  29  additional  64-bit  event  counters, mhpmcounter3 -mhpmcounter31 . The event selector CSRs, mhpmevent3 -mhpmevent31 , are 64-bit WARL registers that control which event causes the corresponding counter to increment. The meaning of these events is defined by the platform,  but  event  0  is  defined  to  mean  "no  event."  All  counters  should  be  implemented,  but  a  legal implementation is to make both the counter and its corresponding event selector be read-only 0.

Figure 17. Hardware performance monitor counters.

<image>

The mhpmcounters are WARL registers that support up to 64 bits of precision on RV32 and RV64.

When XLEN=32, reads of the mcycle , minstret , mhpmcounter n , and mhpmevent n CSRs return bitj 31-0 of the corresponding register, and writes change only bits 31-0; reads of the mcycleh , minstreth , mhpmcounter n h , and mhpmevent n h CSRs return bits 63-32 of the corresponding register, and writes change only bits 63-32. The mhpmevent n h CSRs are provided only if the Sscofpmf extension is implemented.
============================================================
=========
RESPONSE:
=========
============================================================
- The hardware‑performance monitor provides 29 additional 64‑bit event counters, **mhpmcounter3 – mhpmcounter31**; therefore **mhpmcounter7** is one of these counters and is a 64‑bit counter.  

- **mhpmcounter7** is a **WARL** register that *supports up to 64 bits of precision* on both RV32 and RV64 implementations.  

- After a hart reset, the **mhpmcounter7** register contains an *arbitrary value* and may be written with any value.  

- **Any CSR write** to **mhpmcounter7** *takes effect after the writing instruction has otherwise completed*.  

- The **event‑selector CSR** that controls **mhpmcounter7** is **mhpmevent7**. **mhpmevent7** is a 64‑bit **WARL** register; the value programmed in **mhpmevent7** *determines which event causes mhpmcounter7 to increment*.  

- **Event 0** is defined to mean *"no event."* Consequently, if **mhpmevent7 = 0**, **mhpmcounter7** does **not** increment for any event.  

- A legal implementation may choose to make **mhpmcounter7** and its corresponding selector **mhpmevent7** *read‑only zero*. In such an implementation, reads of **mhpmcounter7** return 0 and writes have no effect.  

- When **XLEN = 32**:  
  * A read of **mhpmcounter7** returns **bits 31‑0** of the 64‑bit counter.  
  * A write to **mhpmcounter7** changes **only bits 31‑0** of the counter.  
  * A read of **mhpmcounter7h** (the high‑half CSR) returns **bits 63‑32** of the counter.  
  * A write to **mhpmcounter7h** changes **only bits 63‑32** of the counter.  

- The above behavior for the low‑half (**mhpmcounter7**) and high‑half (**mhpmcounter7h**) CSRs applies only when the **Sscofpmf** extension is implemented for the high‑half CSRs (the text specifies this requirement for the **mhpmevent** high‑half CSRs; the same requirement is implied for the counter high‑half CSRs).

## 3.1.11. Machine Counter-Enable ( mcounteren ) Register

The counter-enable mcounteren register is a 32-bit register that controls the availability of the hardware performance-monitoring counters to the next-lower privileged mode.

64

64

Figure 18. Counter-enable ( mcounteren ) register.

<image>

The settings in this register only control accessibility. The act of reading or writing this register does not affect the underlying counters, which continue to increment even when not accessible.

When the CY, TM, IR, or HPM n bit  in  the mcounteren register is clear, attempts to read the cycle , time , instret ,  or hpmcountern register  while  executing  in  S-mode  or  U-mode  will  cause  an  illegal-instruction exception.  When  one  of  these  bits  is  set,  access  to  the  corresponding  register  is  permitted  in  the  next implemented privilege mode (S-mode if implemented, otherwise U-mode).

<image>

The counter-enable bits support two common use cases with minimal hardware. For harts that do not need high-performance timers and counters, machine-mode software can trap accesses and  implement  all  features  in  software.  For  harts  that  need  high-performance  timers  and counters  but  are  not  concerned  with  obfuscating  the  underlying  hardware  counters,  the counters can be directly exposed to lower privilege modes.

In  addition,  when  the  TM  bit  in  the mcounteren register  is  clear,  attempts  to  access  the stimecmp or vstimecmp register  while  executing  in  a  mode  less  privileged  than  M  will  cause  an  illegal-instruction exception.  When  this  bit  is  set,  access  to  the stimecmp or vstimecmp register  is  permitted  in  S-mode  if implemented, and access to the vstimecmp register (via stimecmp ) is permitted in VS-mode if implemented and not otherwise prevented by the TM bit in hcounteren .

The cycle , instret ,  and hpmcountern CSRs are read-only shadows of mcycle , minstret ,  and mhpmcounter n ,  respectively. The time CSR is a read-only shadow of the memory-mapped mtime register. Analogously, when  XLEN=32,  the cycleh , instreth and hpmcounternh CSRs  are  read-only  shadows  of mcycleh , minstreth and mhpmcounternh , respectively. When XLEN=32, the timeh CSR is a read-only shadow of the upper 32 bits of the memory-mapped mtime register, while time shadows only the lower 32 bits of mtime .

<image>

Implementations can convert reads of the time and timeh CSRs into loads to the memorymapped mtime register, or emulate this functionality on behalf of less-privileged modes in Mmode software.

In harts with U-mode, the mcounteren must be implemented, but all fields are WARL and may be read-only zero,  indicating  reads  to  the  corresponding  counter  will  cause  an  illegal-instruction  exception  when executing in a less-privileged mode. In harts without U-mode, the mcounteren register should not exist.

## 3.1.12. Machine Counter-Inhibit ( mcountinhibit ) Register

Figure 19. Counter-inhibit mcountinhibit register

<image>

The counter-inhibit register mcountinhibit is a 32-bit WARL register that controls which of the hardware performance-monitoring  counters  increment.  The  settings  in  this  register  only  control  whether  the counters increment; their accessibility is not affected by the setting of this register.

When  the  CY,  IR,  or  HPM n bit  in  the mcountinhibit register  is clear,  the mcycle , minstret ,  or mhpmcountern register increments as usual. When the CY, IR, or HPM n bit is set, the corresponding counter does not increment.

The mcycle CSR may be shared between harts on the same core, in which case the mcountinhibit.CY field is also shared between those harts, and so writes to mcountinhibit.CY will be visible to those harts.

If the mcountinhibit register is not implemented, the implementation behaves as though the register were set to zero.

<image>

When  the mcycle and minstret counters  are  not  needed,  it  is  desirable  to  conditionally inhibit them to reduce energy consumption. Providing a single CSR to inhibit all counters also allows the counters to be atomically sampled.

Because the mtime counter can be shared between multiple cores, it cannot be inhibited with the mcountinhibit mechanism.
============================================================
=========
RESPONSE:
=========
============================================================
- The **mcountinhibit** register is a 32‑bit WARL register that **controls which of the hardware performance‑monitoring counters increment**; its settings **do not affect the counters' accessibility**.  

- **When the HPM7 bit in the mcountinhibit register is clear**, the **mhpmcounter7** register **increments as usual**.  

- **When the HPM7 bit in the mcountinhibit register is set**, the **mhpmcounter7** register **does not increment**.  

- **If the mcountinhibit register is not implemented**, the implementation **behaves as though the register were set to zero**; consequently the HPM7 bit is effectively clear and **mhpmcounter7 increments as usual**.

## 21.1. Count Overflow Control

The following bits are added to mhpmevent :

| 63   | 62   | 61   | 60   | 59    | 58    | 57   | 56   |
|------|------|------|------|-------|-------|------|------|
| OF   | MINH | SINH | UINH | VSINH | VUINH | WPRI | WPRI |

| Field   | Description                                                                  |
|---------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| OF      | Overflow status and interrupt disable bit that is set when counter overflows |
| MINH    | If set, then counting of events in M-mode is inhibited                       |
| SINH    | If set, then counting of events in S/HS-mode is inhibited                    |
| UINH    | If set, then counting of events in U-mode is inhibited                       |
| VSINH   | If set, then counting of events in VS-mode is inhibited                      |
| VUINH   | If set, then counting of events in VU-mode is inhibited                      |
| WPRI    | Reserved                                                                     |
| WPRI    | Reserved                                                                     |

For each x INH bit, if the associated privilege mode is not implemented, the bit is read-only zero.

Each of the five x INH bits, when set, inhibit counting of events while in privilege mode x .  All-zeroes for these bits results in counting of events in all modes.

The OF bit is set when the corresponding hpmcounter overflows, and remains set until written by software. Since hpmcounter  values  are  unsigned  values,  overflow is defined as unsigned  overflow  of  the implemented counter bits. Note that there is no loss of information after an overflow since the counter wraps around and keeps counting while the sticky OF bit remains set.

If supervisor mode is implemented, the 32-bit scountovf register contains read-only shadow copies of the OF bits in all 29 mhpmevent registers.

If an hpmcounter overflows while the associated OF bit is zero, then a "count overflow interrupt request" is generated.  If  the  OF  bit  is  one,  then  no  interrupt  request  is  generated.  Consequently  the  OF  bit  also functions as a count overflow interrupt disable for the associated hpmcounter.

Count  overflow  never  results  from  writes  to  the  mhpmcounter n or  mhpmevent n registers,  only  from hardware increments of counter registers.

This count-overflow-interrupt-request signal is treated as a standard local interrupt that corresponds to bit 13 in the mip / mie / sip / sie registers. The mip / sip LCOFIP and mie / sie LCOFIE bits are, respectively, the interrupt-pending and interrupt-enable bits for this interrupt. ('LCOFI' represents 'Local Count Overflow Interrupt'.)

Generation of a count-overflow-interrupt request by an hpmcounter sets the associated OF bit. When an OF bit is set, it eventually, but not necessarily immediately, sets the LCOFIP bit in the mip / sip registers. The LCOFIP bit is cleared by software before servicing the count overflow interrupt resulting from one or more count overflows. The mideleg register controls the delegation of this interrupt to S-mode versus M-mode.#

<image>

There are not separate overflow status and overflow interrupt enable bits. In practice, enabling overflow interrupt generation (by clearing the OF bit) is done in conjunction with initializing the  counter  to  a  starting  value.  Once  a  counter  has  overflowed,  it  and  the  OF  bit  must  be reinitialized before another overflow interrupt can be generated.

<image>

Software can distinguish newly overflowed counters (yet to be serviced by an overflow interrupt handler) from overflowed counters that have already been serviced or that are configured to not generate an interrupt on overflow, by maintaining a bit mask reflecting which counters are active and due to eventually overflow.

- The **OF bit** in *mhpmevent7* "is set when the corresponding hpmcounter overflows, and remains set until written by software."  
  *Effect:* When *mhpmcounter7* overflows, its associated OF bit becomes 1 and stays 1 until software clears it.

- **Overflow definition:** "Since hpmcounter values are unsigned values, overflow is defined as unsigned overflow of the implemented counter bits."  
  *Effect:* An overflow of *mhpmcounter7* occurs when its unsigned value wraps past the most‑significant implemented bit.

- **Counter wrap‑around:** "Note that there is no loss of information after an overflow since the counter wraps around and keeps counting while the sticky OF bit remains set."  
  *Effect:* After *mhpmcounter7* overflows, it continues counting from zero (or the wrapped value) while its OF bit stays set.

- **Supervisor shadow register:** "If supervisor mode is implemented, the 32‑bit scountovf register contains read‑only shadow copies of the OF bits in all 29 mhpmevent registers."  
  *Effect:* The OF bit for *mhpmevent7* is reflected as a read‑only bit in *scountovf*.

- **Count‑overflow interrupt generation:**  
  – "If an hpmcounter overflows while the associated OF bit is zero, then a 'count overflow interrupt request' is generated."  
  – "If the OF bit is one, then no interrupt request is generated."  
  *Effect:* When *mhpmcounter7* overflows and its OF bit is 0, a count‑overflow interrupt request is raised; if the OF bit is already 1, no interrupt request is raised.

- **Interrupt‑disable role of OF:** "Consequently the OF bit also functions as a count overflow interrupt disable for the associated hpmcounter."  
  *Effect:* Setting the OF bit in *mhpmevent7* disables further overflow interrupt requests for *mhpmcounter7*.

- **Source of overflow:** "Count overflow never results from writes to the mhpmcounter n or mhpmevent n registers, only from hardware increments of counter registers."  
  *Effect:* *mhpmcounter7* can overflow only due to hardware increments, never due to a software write to *mhpmcounter7* or *mhpmevent7*.

  *Effect:* When *mhpmcounter7* causes an overflow interrupt, its OF bit is set and later the LCOFIP bit becomes pending.

  *Effect:* To allow *mhpmcounter7* to generate another overflow interrupt, software must clear its OF bit and re‑initialize the counter.

  *Effect:* After *mhpmcounter7* overflows, both the counter value and its OF bit must be written to restart overflow‑interrupt generation.

  *Effect:* Software may track *mhpmcounter7* in a bit mask to know whether it is awaiting service or has been handled.

- **INH bits in mhpmevent7:**  
  – "MINH, SINH, UINH, VSINH, VUINH … inhibit counting of events while in privilege mode x. All‑zeroes for these bits results in counting of events in all modes."  
  – "For each x INH bit, if the associated privilege mode is not implemented, the bit is read‑only zero."

## 3.1.10. Hardware Performance Monitor

M-mode includes a basic hardware performance-monitoring facility. The mcycle CSR counts the number of clock cycles executed by the processor core on which the hart is running. The minstret CSR counts the number of instructions the hart has retired. The mcycle and minstret registers have 64-bit precision on all RV32 and RV64 harts.

The counter registers have an arbitrary value after the hart is reset, and can be written with a given value. Any CSR write takes effect after the writing instruction has otherwise completed. The mcycle CSR may be shared between harts on the same core, in which case writes to mcycle will be visible to those harts. The platform should provide a mechanism to indicate which harts share an mcycle CSR.

The  hardware  performance  monitor  includes  29  additional  64-bit  event  counters, mhpmcounter3 -mhpmcounter31 . The event selector CSRs, mhpmevent3 -mhpmevent31 , are 64-bit WARL registers that control which event causes the corresponding counter to increment. The meaning of these events is defined by the platform,  but  event  0  is  defined  to  mean  "no  event."  All  counters  should  be  implemented,  but  a  legal implementation is to make both the counter and its corresponding event selector be read-only 0.

Figure 17. Hardware performance monitor counters.

<image>

The mhpmcounters are WARL registers that support up to 64 bits of precision on RV32 and RV64.

## 3.1.11. Machine Counter-Enable ( mcounteren ) Register

The counter-enable mcounteren register is a 32-bit register that controls the availability of the hardware performance-monitoring counters to the next-lower privileged mode.

64

64

Figure 18. Counter-enable ( mcounteren ) register.

<image>

The settings in this register only control accessibility. The act of reading or writing this register does not affect the underlying counters, which continue to increment even when not accessible.

When the CY, TM, IR, or HPM n bit  in  the mcounteren register is clear, attempts to read the cycle , time , instret ,  or hpmcountern register  while  executing  in  S-mode  or  U-mode  will  cause  an  illegal-instruction exception.  When  one  of  these  bits  is  set,  access  to  the  corresponding  register  is  permitted  in  the  next implemented privilege mode (S-mode if implemented, otherwise U-mode).

<image>

The counter-enable bits support two common use cases with minimal hardware. For harts that do not need high-performance timers and counters, machine-mode software can trap accesses and  implement  all  features  in  software.  For  harts  that  need  high-performance  timers  and counters  but  are  not  concerned  with  obfuscating  the  underlying  hardware  counters,  the counters can be directly exposed to lower privilege modes.

In  addition,  when  the  TM  bit  in  the mcounteren register  is  clear,  attempts  to  access  the stimecmp or vstimecmp register  while  executing  in  a  mode  less  privileged  than  M  will  cause  an  illegal-instruction exception.  When  this  bit  is  set,  access  to  the stimecmp or vstimecmp register  is  permitted  in  S-mode  if implemented, and access to the vstimecmp register (via stimecmp ) is permitted in VS-mode if implemented and not otherwise prevented by the TM bit in hcounteren .

The cycle , instret ,  and hpmcountern CSRs are read-only shadows of mcycle , minstret ,  and mhpmcounter n ,  respectively. The time CSR is a read-only shadow of the memory-mapped mtime register. Analogously, when  XLEN=32,  the cycleh , instreth and hpmcounternh CSRs  are  read-only  shadows  of mcycleh , minstreth and mhpmcounternh , respectively. When XLEN=32, the timeh CSR is a read-only shadow of the upper 32 bits of the memory-mapped mtime register, while time shadows only the lower 32 bits of mtime .

<image>

Implementations can convert reads of the time and timeh CSRs into loads to the memorymapped mtime register, or emulate this functionality on behalf of less-privileged modes in Mmode software.

In harts with U-mode, the mcounteren must be implemented, but all fields are WARL and may be read-only zero,  indicating  reads  to  the  corresponding  counter  will  cause  an  illegal-instruction  exception  when executing in a less-privileged mode. In harts without U-mode, the mcounteren register should not exist.

## 3.1.12. Machine Counter-Inhibit ( mcountinhibit ) Register

Figure 19. Counter-inhibit mcountinhibit register

<image>

The counter-inhibit register mcountinhibit is a 32-bit WARL register that controls which of the hardware performance-monitoring  counters  increment.  The  settings  in  this  register  only  control  whether  the counters increment; their accessibility is not affected by the setting of this register.

When  the  CY,  IR,  or  HPM n bit  in  the mcountinhibit register  is clear,  the mcycle , minstret ,  or mhpmcountern register increments as usual. When the CY, IR, or HPM n bit is set, the corresponding counter does not increment.

The mcycle CSR may be shared between harts on the same core, in which case the mcountinhibit.CY field is also shared between those harts, and so writes to mcountinhibit.CY will be visible to those harts.

If the mcountinhibit register is not implemented, the implementation behaves as though the register were set to zero.

<image>

When  the mcycle and minstret counters  are  not  needed,  it  is  desirable  to  conditionally inhibit them to reduce energy consumption. Providing a single CSR to inhibit all counters also allows the counters to be atomically sampled.

Because the mtime counter can be shared between multiple cores, it cannot be inhibited with the mcountinhibit mechanism.
============================================================
=========
RESPONSE:
=========
============================================================
- When the **HPM 8** bit in the **mcountinhibit** register is **clear**, the **mhpmcounter8** register **increments as usual**.  
- When the **HPM 8** bit in the **mcountinhibit** register is **set**, the **mhpmcounter8** register **does not increment**.  

- The **mcountinhibit** register **only controls whether the counters increment; their accessibility is not affected** by the setting of this register.  

- **If the mcountinhibit register is not implemented**, the implementation **behaves as though the register were set to zero**, so the **mhpmcounter8** register **increments**.

## 5.2. Machine-level CSRs

| Number   | Privilege   | Width   | Name     | Description                       |
|----------|-------------|---------|----------|-----------------------------------|
| 0x350    | MRW         | XLEN    | miselect | Machine indirect register select  |
| 0x351    | MRW         | XLEN    | mireg    | Machine indirect register alias   |
| 0x352    | MRW         | XLEN    | mireg2   | Machine indirect register alias 2 |
| 0x353    | MRW         | XLEN    | mireg3   | Machine indirect register alias 3 |
| 0x355    | MRW         | XLEN    | mireg4   | Machine indirect register alias 4 |
| 0x356    | MRW         | XLEN    | mireg5   | Machine indirect register alias 5 |
| 0x357    | MRW         | XLEN    | mireg6   | Machine indirect register alias 6 |

<image>

The mireg* CSR numbers are not consecutive because miph is CSR number 0x354.

The CSRs listed in the table above provide a window for accessing register state indirectly. The value of miselect determines which register is accessed upon read or write of each of the machine indirect alias CSRs ( mireg* ). miselect value  ranges  are  allocated  to  dependent  extensions,  which  specify  the  register state accessible via each mireg i register, for each miselect value. miselect is a WARL register.

The miselect register  implements  at  least  enough  bits  to  support  all  implemented miselect values (corresponding to the implemented extensions that utilize miselect / mireg* to  indirectly  access  register state). The miselect register may be read-only zero if there are no extensions implemented that utilize it.

Values of miselect with the most-significant bit set (bit XLEN - 1 = 1) are designated only for custom use, presumably  for  accessing  custom  registers  through  the  alias  CSRs.  Values  of miselect with  the  mostsignificant  bit  clear  are  designated  only  for  standard  use  and  are  reserved  until  allocated  to  a  standard architecture extension. If XLEN is changed, the most-significant bit of miselect moves to the new position, retaining its value from before.

<image>

An implementation is not required to support any custom values for miselect .

The behavior upon accessing mireg* from M-mode, while miselect holds a value that is not implemented, is UNSPECIFIED.

<image>

It is expected that implementations will typically raise an illegal-instruction exception for such accesses, so that, for example, they can be identified as software bugs. Platform specs, profile specs,  and/or  the  Privileged  ISA  spec  may  place  more  restrictions  on  behavior  for  such accesses.

Attempts to access mireg* while miselect holds a number in an allocated and implemented range results in a specific behavior that, for each combination of miselect and mireg i ,  is  defined by the extension to which the miselect value is allocated.

Ordinarily, each mireg i will access register state, access read-only 0 state, or raise an illegalinstruction exception.

<image>

<image>

For  RV32,  if  an  extension  defines  an  indirectly  accessed  register  as  64  bits  wide,  it  is recommended that the lower 32 bits of the register are accessed through one of mireg , mireg2 , or mireg3 ,  while  the  upper  32  bits  are  accessed  through mireg4 , mireg5 ,  or mireg6 , respectively.

Six *ireg* registers are defined in order to ensure that the needs of extensions in development are covered, with some room for growth. For example, for an siselect value associated with counter X, sireg / sireg2 could be used to access mhpmcounterX / mhpmeventX ,  while sireg4 / sireg5 could access mhpmcounterXh / mhpmeventXh . Six *ireg* registers allows for accessing up to  3  CSR  arrays  per  index  ( *iselect )  with  RV32-only  CSRs,  or  up  to  6  CSR  arrays  per index value without RV32-only CSRs.
============================================================

## 21.1. Count Overflow Control

The following bits are added to mhpmevent :

| 63   | 62   | 61   | 60   | 59    | 58    | 57   | 56   |
|------|------|------|------|-------|-------|------|------|
| OF   | MINH | SINH | UINH | VSINH | VUINH | WPRI | WPRI |

| Field   | Description                                                                  |
|---------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| OF      | Overflow status and interrupt disable bit that is set when counter overflows |
| MINH    | If set, then counting of events in M-mode is inhibited                       |
| SINH    | If set, then counting of events in S/HS-mode is inhibited                    |
| UINH    | If set, then counting of events in U-mode is inhibited                       |
| VSINH   | If set, then counting of events in VS-mode is inhibited                      |
| VUINH   | If set, then counting of events in VU-mode is inhibited                      |
| WPRI    | Reserved                                                                     |
| WPRI    | Reserved                                                                     |

For each x INH bit, if the associated privilege mode is not implemented, the bit is read-only zero.

Each of the five x INH bits, when set, inhibit counting of events while in privilege mode x .  All-zeroes for these bits results in counting of events in all modes.

The OF bit is set when the corresponding hpmcounter overflows, and remains set until written by software. Since hpmcounter  values  are  unsigned  values,  overflow is defined as unsigned  overflow  of  the implemented counter bits. Note that there is no loss of information after an overflow since the counter wraps around and keeps counting while the sticky OF bit remains set.

If supervisor mode is implemented, the 32-bit scountovf register contains read-only shadow copies of the OF bits in all 29 mhpmevent registers.

If an hpmcounter overflows while the associated OF bit is zero, then a "count overflow interrupt request" is generated.  If  the  OF  bit  is  one,  then  no  interrupt  request  is  generated.  Consequently  the  OF  bit  also functions as a count overflow interrupt disable for the associated hpmcounter.

Count  overflow  never  results  from  writes  to  the  mhpmcounter n or  mhpmevent n registers,  only  from hardware increments of counter registers.

This count-overflow-interrupt-request signal is treated as a standard local interrupt that corresponds to bit 13 in the mip / mie / sip / sie registers. The mip / sip LCOFIP and mie / sie LCOFIE bits are, respectively, the interrupt-pending and interrupt-enable bits for this interrupt. ('LCOFI' represents 'Local Count Overflow Interrupt'.)

Generation of a count-overflow-interrupt request by an hpmcounter sets the associated OF bit. When an OF bit is set, it eventually, but not necessarily immediately, sets the LCOFIP bit in the mip / sip registers. The LCOFIP bit is cleared by software before servicing the count overflow interrupt resulting from one or more count overflows. The mideleg register controls the delegation of this interrupt to S-mode versus M-mode.#

<image>

There are not separate overflow status and overflow interrupt enable bits. In practice, enabling overflow interrupt generation (by clearing the OF bit) is done in conjunction with initializing the  counter  to  a  starting  value.  Once  a  counter  has  overflowed,  it  and  the  OF  bit  must  be reinitialized before another overflow interrupt can be generated.

<image>

Software can distinguish newly overflowed counters (yet to be serviced by an overflow interrupt handler) from overflowed counters that have already been serviced or that are configured to not generate an interrupt on overflow, by maintaining a bit mask reflecting which counters are active and due to eventually overflow.
============================================================

## 3.1.10. Hardware Performance Monitor

M-mode includes a basic hardware performance-monitoring facility. The mcycle CSR counts the number of clock cycles executed by the processor core on which the hart is running. The minstret CSR counts the number of instructions the hart has retired. The mcycle and minstret registers have 64-bit precision on all RV32 and RV64 harts.

The counter registers have an arbitrary value after the hart is reset, and can be written with a given value. Any CSR write takes effect after the writing instruction has otherwise completed. The mcycle CSR may be shared between harts on the same core, in which case writes to mcycle will be visible to those harts. The platform should provide a mechanism to indicate which harts share an mcycle CSR.

The  hardware  performance  monitor  includes  29  additional  64-bit  event  counters, mhpmcounter3 -mhpmcounter31 . The event selector CSRs, mhpmevent3 -mhpmevent31 , are 64-bit WARL registers that control which event causes the corresponding counter to increment. The meaning of these events is defined by the platform,  but  event  0  is  defined  to  mean  "no  event."  All  counters  should  be  implemented,  but  a  legal implementation is to make both the counter and its corresponding event selector be read-only 0.

Figure 17. Hardware performance monitor counters.

<image>

The mhpmcounters are WARL registers that support up to 64 bits of precision on RV32 and RV64.

When XLEN=32, reads of the mcycle , minstret , mhpmcounter n , and mhpmevent n CSRs return bitj 31-0 of the corresponding register, and writes change only bits 31-0; reads of the mcycleh , minstreth , mhpmcounter n h , and mhpmevent n h CSRs return bits 63-32 of the corresponding register, and writes change only bits 63-32. The mhpmevent n h CSRs are provided only if the Sscofpmf extension is implemented.
============================================================
=========
RESPONSE:
=========
============================================================
- The hardware‑performance‑monitor facility provides 29 additional 64‑bit event counters, **mhpmcounter3‑mhpmcounter31**; therefore **mhpmcounter9** is one of these counters.  

- **mhpmcounter9** is a **WARL** register that **supports up to 64 bits of precision on RV32 and RV64**.  

- After a hart reset, **mhpmcounter9** has an arbitrary value, and it **can be written with a given value**.  

- **Any CSR write to mhpmcounter9 takes effect after the writing instruction has otherwise completed**.  

- The **event‑selector CSR mhpmevent9** is a **64‑bit WARL register that controls which event causes mhpmcounter9 to increment**.  

- **The meaning of the events selected by mhpmevent9 is defined by the platform, but event 0 is defined to mean "no event."**  

- **All counters should be implemented, but a legal implementation is to make both the counter and its corresponding event selector be read‑only 0**; thus a legal implementation may have **mhpmcounter9 = 0** and **mhpmevent9 = 0** (read‑only).  

- **When XLEN = 32**:  
  * A read of **mhpmcounter9** returns **bits 31‑0** of the corresponding 64‑bit register, and a write to **mhpmcounter9** **changes only bits 31‑0**.  
  * A read of **mhpmcounter9h** (the high‑half CSR) returns **bits 63‑32**, and a write to **mhpmcounter9h** **changes only bits 63‑32**.  

- The **mhpmcounter9h** CSR (the high‑half of mhpmcounter9) exists only when the **Sscofpmf** extension is implemented; otherwise only the low‑half CSR (**mhpmcounter9**) is present.  

- The **mhpmevent9h** CSR (high‑half of the event selector) is provided **only if the Sscofpmf extension is implemented**; it forms part of the 64‑bit value that selects the event for **mhpmcounter9**.

## 3.1.11. Machine Counter-Enable ( mcounteren ) Register

The counter-enable mcounteren register is a 32-bit register that controls the availability of the hardware performance-monitoring counters to the next-lower privileged mode.

64

64

Figure 18. Counter-enable ( mcounteren ) register.

<image>

The settings in this register only control accessibility. The act of reading or writing this register does not affect the underlying counters, which continue to increment even when not accessible.

When the CY, TM, IR, or HPM n bit  in  the mcounteren register is clear, attempts to read the cycle , time , instret ,  or hpmcountern register  while  executing  in  S-mode  or  U-mode  will  cause  an  illegal-instruction exception.  When  one  of  these  bits  is  set,  access  to  the  corresponding  register  is  permitted  in  the  next implemented privilege mode (S-mode if implemented, otherwise U-mode).

<image>

The counter-enable bits support two common use cases with minimal hardware. For harts that do not need high-performance timers and counters, machine-mode software can trap accesses and  implement  all  features  in  software.  For  harts  that  need  high-performance  timers  and counters  but  are  not  concerned  with  obfuscating  the  underlying  hardware  counters,  the counters can be directly exposed to lower privilege modes.

In  addition,  when  the  TM  bit  in  the mcounteren register  is  clear,  attempts  to  access  the stimecmp or vstimecmp register  while  executing  in  a  mode  less  privileged  than  M  will  cause  an  illegal-instruction exception.  When  this  bit  is  set,  access  to  the stimecmp or vstimecmp register  is  permitted  in  S-mode  if implemented, and access to the vstimecmp register (via stimecmp ) is permitted in VS-mode if implemented and not otherwise prevented by the TM bit in hcounteren .

The cycle , instret ,  and hpmcountern CSRs are read-only shadows of mcycle , minstret ,  and mhpmcounter n ,  respectively. The time CSR is a read-only shadow of the memory-mapped mtime register. Analogously, when  XLEN=32,  the cycleh , instreth and hpmcounternh CSRs  are  read-only  shadows  of mcycleh , minstreth and mhpmcounternh , respectively. When XLEN=32, the timeh CSR is a read-only shadow of the upper 32 bits of the memory-mapped mtime register, while time shadows only the lower 32 bits of mtime .

<image>

Implementations can convert reads of the time and timeh CSRs into loads to the memorymapped mtime register, or emulate this functionality on behalf of less-privileged modes in Mmode software.

In harts with U-mode, the mcounteren must be implemented, but all fields are WARL and may be read-only zero,  indicating  reads  to  the  corresponding  counter  will  cause  an  illegal-instruction  exception  when executing in a less-privileged mode. In harts without U-mode, the mcounteren register should not exist.

## 3.1.12. Machine Counter-Inhibit ( mcountinhibit ) Register

Figure 19. Counter-inhibit mcountinhibit register

<image>

The counter-inhibit register mcountinhibit is a 32-bit WARL register that controls which of the hardware performance-monitoring  counters  increment.  The  settings  in  this  register  only  control  whether  the counters increment; their accessibility is not affected by the setting of this register.

When  the  CY,  IR,  or  HPM n bit  in  the mcountinhibit register  is clear,  the mcycle , minstret ,  or mhpmcountern register increments as usual. When the CY, IR, or HPM n bit is set, the corresponding counter does not increment.

The mcycle CSR may be shared between harts on the same core, in which case the mcountinhibit.CY field is also shared between those harts, and so writes to mcountinhibit.CY will be visible to those harts.

If the mcountinhibit register is not implemented, the implementation behaves as though the register were set to zero.

<image>

When  the mcycle and minstret counters  are  not  needed,  it  is  desirable  to  conditionally inhibit them to reduce energy consumption. Providing a single CSR to inhibit all counters also allows the counters to be atomically sampled.

Because the mtime counter can be shared between multiple cores, it cannot be inhibited with the mcountinhibit mechanism.
============================================================
=========
RESPONSE:
=========
============================================================
- The **mcountinhibit** CSR is a 32‑bit WARL register that **controls which of the hardware performance‑monitoring counters increment**; it does **not affect the accessibility** of those counters.  

- **mhpmcounter9** is one of the "mhpmcountern" registers referenced by the generic rule "HPM n".  

- **Increment behavior**:  
  - **When the HPM 9 bit in the mcountinhibit register is clear**, the **mhpmcounter9 register increments as usual**.  
  - **When the HPM 9 bit in the mcountinhibit register is set**, the **mhpmcounter9 register does not increment**.  

- **Implementation fallback**:  
  - **If the mcountinhibit register is not implemented**, the implementation **behaves as though the register were set to zero**, which means the HPM 9 bit is treated as clear and **mhpmcounter9 increments as usual**.

## 5.2. Machine-level CSRs

| Number   | Privilege   | Width   | Name     | Description                       |
|----------|-------------|---------|----------|-----------------------------------|
| 0x350    | MRW         | XLEN    | miselect | Machine indirect register select  |
| 0x351    | MRW         | XLEN    | mireg    | Machine indirect register alias   |
| 0x352    | MRW         | XLEN    | mireg2   | Machine indirect register alias 2 |
| 0x353    | MRW         | XLEN    | mireg3   | Machine indirect register alias 3 |
| 0x355    | MRW         | XLEN    | mireg4   | Machine indirect register alias 4 |
| 0x356    | MRW         | XLEN    | mireg5   | Machine indirect register alias 5 |
| 0x357    | MRW         | XLEN    | mireg6   | Machine indirect register alias 6 |

<image>

The mireg* CSR numbers are not consecutive because miph is CSR number 0x354.

The CSRs listed in the table above provide a window for accessing register state indirectly. The value of miselect determines which register is accessed upon read or write of each of the machine indirect alias CSRs ( mireg* ). miselect value  ranges  are  allocated  to  dependent  extensions,  which  specify  the  register state accessible via each mireg i register, for each miselect value. miselect is a WARL register.

The miselect register  implements  at  least  enough  bits  to  support  all  implemented miselect values (corresponding to the implemented extensions that utilize miselect / mireg* to  indirectly  access  register state). The miselect register may be read-only zero if there are no extensions implemented that utilize it.

Values of miselect with the most-significant bit set (bit XLEN - 1 = 1) are designated only for custom use, presumably  for  accessing  custom  registers  through  the  alias  CSRs.  Values  of miselect with  the  mostsignificant  bit  clear  are  designated  only  for  standard  use  and  are  reserved  until  allocated  to  a  standard architecture extension. If XLEN is changed, the most-significant bit of miselect moves to the new position, retaining its value from before.

<image>

An implementation is not required to support any custom values for miselect .

The behavior upon accessing mireg* from M-mode, while miselect holds a value that is not implemented, is UNSPECIFIED.

<image>

It is expected that implementations will typically raise an illegal-instruction exception for such accesses, so that, for example, they can be identified as software bugs. Platform specs, profile specs,  and/or  the  Privileged  ISA  spec  may  place  more  restrictions  on  behavior  for  such accesses.

Attempts to access mireg* while miselect holds a number in an allocated and implemented range results in a specific behavior that, for each combination of miselect and mireg i ,  is  defined by the extension to which the miselect value is allocated.

Ordinarily, each mireg i will access register state, access read-only 0 state, or raise an illegalinstruction exception.

<image>

<image>

For  RV32,  if  an  extension  defines  an  indirectly  accessed  register  as  64  bits  wide,  it  is recommended that the lower 32 bits of the register are accessed through one of mireg , mireg2 , or mireg3 ,  while  the  upper  32  bits  are  accessed  through mireg4 , mireg5 ,  or mireg6 , respectively.

Six *ireg* registers are defined in order to ensure that the needs of extensions in development are covered, with some room for growth. For example, for an siselect value associated with counter X, sireg / sireg2 could be used to access mhpmcounterX / mhpmeventX ,  while sireg4 / sireg5 could access mhpmcounterXh / mhpmeventXh . Six *ireg* registers allows for accessing up to  3  CSR  arrays  per  index  ( *iselect )  with  RV32-only  CSRs,  or  up  to  6  CSR  arrays  per index value without RV32-only CSRs.
============================================================
=========
RESPONSE:
=========
============================================================
- For an **siselect** value associated with counter 9, **sireg** or **sireg2** could be used to access **mhpmcounter9** (and the corresponding **mhpmevent9**) ; **sireg4** or **sireg5** could be used to access **mhpmcounter9h** (and the corresponding **mhpmevent9h**).  

- For RV32, **if an extension defines an indirectly accessed register as 64 bits wide**, it is *recommended* that the lower 32 bits of the register are accessed through one of **mireg**, **mireg2**, or **mireg3**, while the upper 32 bits are accessed through **mireg4**, **mireg5**, or **mireg6**, respectively.  Consequently, if **mhpmcounter9** is such a 64‑bit indirectly accessed register, its lower half could be accessed via **mireg\*** and its upper half via **mireg4‑6**.  

- **Attempts to access mireg\*** while **miselect** holds a number in an allocated and implemented range "result in a specific behavior that, for each combination of miselect and mireg i, is defined by the extension to which the miselect value is allocated."  Therefore, accessing **mhpmcounter9** indirectly through **mireg\*** is subject to the behavior defined by the extension that allocated the corresponding **miselect** value.  

- **The behavior upon accessing mireg\*** from M‑mode **while miselect holds a value that is not implemented** is **UNSPECIFIED**.  Thus, if **mhpmcounter9** is accessed via **mireg\*** and **miselect** contains an unimplemented value, the resulting behavior is unspecified.  

- It is *expected* (non‑normative) that implementations will typically raise an **illegal‑instruction exception** for accesses to **mireg\*** when **miselect** holds an unimplemented value, so that such accesses can be identified as software bugs.  (This expectation applies to any indirect access, including a possible indirect access to **mhpmcounter9**.)

## 21.1. Count Overflow Control

The following bits are added to mhpmevent :

| 63   | 62   | 61   | 60   | 59    | 58    | 57   | 56   |
|------|------|------|------|-------|-------|------|------|
| OF   | MINH | SINH | UINH | VSINH | VUINH | WPRI | WPRI |

| Field   | Description                                                                  |
|---------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| OF      | Overflow status and interrupt disable bit that is set when counter overflows |
| MINH    | If set, then counting of events in M-mode is inhibited                       |
| SINH    | If set, then counting of events in S/HS-mode is inhibited                    |
| UINH    | If set, then counting of events in U-mode is inhibited                       |
| VSINH   | If set, then counting of events in VS-mode is inhibited                      |
| VUINH   | If set, then counting of events in VU-mode is inhibited                      |
| WPRI    | Reserved                                                                     |
| WPRI    | Reserved                                                                     |

For each x INH bit, if the associated privilege mode is not implemented, the bit is read-only zero.

Each of the five x INH bits, when set, inhibit counting of events while in privilege mode x .  All-zeroes for these bits results in counting of events in all modes.

The OF bit is set when the corresponding hpmcounter overflows, and remains set until written by software. Since hpmcounter  values  are  unsigned  values,  overflow is defined as unsigned  overflow  of  the implemented counter bits. Note that there is no loss of information after an overflow since the counter wraps around and keeps counting while the sticky OF bit remains set.

If supervisor mode is implemented, the 32-bit scountovf register contains read-only shadow copies of the OF bits in all 29 mhpmevent registers.

If an hpmcounter overflows while the associated OF bit is zero, then a "count overflow interrupt request" is generated.  If  the  OF  bit  is  one,  then  no  interrupt  request  is  generated.  Consequently  the  OF  bit  also functions as a count overflow interrupt disable for the associated hpmcounter.

Count  overflow  never  results  from  writes  to  the  mhpmcounter n or  mhpmevent n registers,  only  from hardware increments of counter registers.

This count-overflow-interrupt-request signal is treated as a standard local interrupt that corresponds to bit 13 in the mip / mie / sip / sie registers. The mip / sip LCOFIP and mie / sie LCOFIE bits are, respectively, the interrupt-pending and interrupt-enable bits for this interrupt. ('LCOFI' represents 'Local Count Overflow Interrupt'.)

Generation of a count-overflow-interrupt request by an hpmcounter sets the associated OF bit. When an OF bit is set, it eventually, but not necessarily immediately, sets the LCOFIP bit in the mip / sip registers. The LCOFIP bit is cleared by software before servicing the count overflow interrupt resulting from one or more count overflows. The mideleg register controls the delegation of this interrupt to S-mode versus M-mode.#

<image>

There are not separate overflow status and overflow interrupt enable bits. In practice, enabling overflow interrupt generation (by clearing the OF bit) is done in conjunction with initializing the  counter  to  a  starting  value.  Once  a  counter  has  overflowed,  it  and  the  OF  bit  must  be reinitialized before another overflow interrupt can be generated.

<image>

Software can distinguish newly overflowed counters (yet to be serviced by an overflow interrupt handler) from overflowed counters that have already been serviced or that are configured to not generate an interrupt on overflow, by maintaining a bit mask reflecting which counters are active and due to eventually overflow.
============================================================

## 3.1.10. Hardware Performance Monitor

M-mode includes a basic hardware performance-monitoring facility. The mcycle CSR counts the number of clock cycles executed by the processor core on which the hart is running. The minstret CSR counts the number of instructions the hart has retired. The mcycle and minstret registers have 64-bit precision on all RV32 and RV64 harts.

The counter registers have an arbitrary value after the hart is reset, and can be written with a given value. Any CSR write takes effect after the writing instruction has otherwise completed. The mcycle CSR may be shared between harts on the same core, in which case writes to mcycle will be visible to those harts. The platform should provide a mechanism to indicate which harts share an mcycle CSR.

The  hardware  performance  monitor  includes  29  additional  64-bit  event  counters, mhpmcounter3 -mhpmcounter31 . The event selector CSRs, mhpmevent3 -mhpmevent31 , are 64-bit WARL registers that control which event causes the corresponding counter to increment. The meaning of these events is defined by the platform,  but  event  0  is  defined  to  mean  "no  event."  All  counters  should  be  implemented,  but  a  legal implementation is to make both the counter and its corresponding event selector be read-only 0.

Figure 17. Hardware performance monitor counters.

<image>

The mhpmcounters are WARL registers that support up to 64 bits of precision on RV32 and RV64.

When XLEN=32, reads of the mcycle , minstret , mhpmcounter n , and mhpmevent n CSRs return bitj 31-0 of the corresponding register, and writes change only bits 31-0; reads of the mcycleh , minstreth , mhpmcounter n h , and mhpmevent n h CSRs return bits 63-32 of the corresponding register, and writes change only bits 63-32. The mhpmevent n h CSRs are provided only if the Sscofpmf extension is implemented.

## 3.1.11. Machine Counter-Enable ( mcounteren ) Register

The counter-enable mcounteren register is a 32-bit register that controls the availability of the hardware performance-monitoring counters to the next-lower privileged mode.

64

64

Figure 18. Counter-enable ( mcounteren ) register.

<image>

The settings in this register only control accessibility. The act of reading or writing this register does not affect the underlying counters, which continue to increment even when not accessible.

When the CY, TM, IR, or HPM n bit  in  the mcounteren register is clear, attempts to read the cycle , time , instret ,  or hpmcountern register  while  executing  in  S-mode  or  U-mode  will  cause  an  illegal-instruction exception.  When  one  of  these  bits  is  set,  access  to  the  corresponding  register  is  permitted  in  the  next implemented privilege mode (S-mode if implemented, otherwise U-mode).

<image>

The counter-enable bits support two common use cases with minimal hardware. For harts that do not need high-performance timers and counters, machine-mode software can trap accesses and  implement  all  features  in  software.  For  harts  that  need  high-performance  timers  and counters  but  are  not  concerned  with  obfuscating  the  underlying  hardware  counters,  the counters can be directly exposed to lower privilege modes.

In  addition,  when  the  TM  bit  in  the mcounteren register  is  clear,  attempts  to  access  the stimecmp or vstimecmp register  while  executing  in  a  mode  less  privileged  than  M  will  cause  an  illegal-instruction exception.  When  this  bit  is  set,  access  to  the stimecmp or vstimecmp register  is  permitted  in  S-mode  if implemented, and access to the vstimecmp register (via stimecmp ) is permitted in VS-mode if implemented and not otherwise prevented by the TM bit in hcounteren .

The cycle , instret ,  and hpmcountern CSRs are read-only shadows of mcycle , minstret ,  and mhpmcounter n ,  respectively. The time CSR is a read-only shadow of the memory-mapped mtime register. Analogously, when  XLEN=32,  the cycleh , instreth and hpmcounternh CSRs  are  read-only  shadows  of mcycleh , minstreth and mhpmcounternh , respectively. When XLEN=32, the timeh CSR is a read-only shadow of the upper 32 bits of the memory-mapped mtime register, while time shadows only the lower 32 bits of mtime .

<image>

Implementations can convert reads of the time and timeh CSRs into loads to the memorymapped mtime register, or emulate this functionality on behalf of less-privileged modes in Mmode software.

In harts with U-mode, the mcounteren must be implemented, but all fields are WARL and may be read-only zero,  indicating  reads  to  the  corresponding  counter  will  cause  an  illegal-instruction  exception  when executing in a less-privileged mode. In harts without U-mode, the mcounteren register should not exist.
============================================================
=========

=========

  *When the HPM 10 bit in the mcounteren register is clear, attempts to read the **hpmcounter10** CSR while executing in S‑mode or U‑mode will cause an illegal‑instruction exception.*  
  *When the HPM 10 bit in the mcounteren register is set, access to the **hpmcounter10** CSR is permitted in the next implemented privilege mode (S‑mode if implemented, otherwise U‑mode).*

## 3.1.12. Machine Counter-Inhibit ( mcountinhibit ) Register

Figure 19. Counter-inhibit mcountinhibit register

<image>

The counter-inhibit register mcountinhibit is a 32-bit WARL register that controls which of the hardware performance-monitoring  counters  increment.  The  settings  in  this  register  only  control  whether  the counters increment; their accessibility is not affected by the setting of this register.

When  the  CY,  IR,  or  HPM n bit  in  the mcountinhibit register  is clear,  the mcycle , minstret ,  or mhpmcountern register increments as usual. When the CY, IR, or HPM n bit is set, the corresponding counter does not increment.

The mcycle CSR may be shared between harts on the same core, in which case the mcountinhibit.CY field is also shared between those harts, and so writes to mcountinhibit.CY will be visible to those harts.

If the mcountinhibit register is not implemented, the implementation behaves as though the register were set to zero.

<image>

When  the mcycle and minstret counters  are  not  needed,  it  is  desirable  to  conditionally inhibit them to reduce energy consumption. Providing a single CSR to inhibit all counters also allows the counters to be atomically sampled.

Because the mtime counter can be shared between multiple cores, it cannot be inhibited with the mcountinhibit mechanism.
============================================================

RESPONSE:
=========

- **When the HPM10 bit in the mcountinhibit register is clear**, the **mhpmcounter10** register **increments as usual**.  

- **When the HPM10 bit in the mcountinhibit register is set**, the **mhpmcounter10** register **does not increment**.  

- If the **mcountinhibit** register is **not implemented**, the implementation **behaves as though the register were set to zero**; consequently the HPM10 bit is treated as clear and **mhpmcounter10 increments as usual**.

## 21.1. Count Overflow Control

The following bits are added to mhpmevent :

| 63   | 62   | 61   | 60   | 59    | 58    | 57   | 56   |
|------|------|------|------|-------|-------|------|------|
| OF   | MINH | SINH | UINH | VSINH | VUINH | WPRI | WPRI |

| Field   | Description                                                                  |
|---------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| OF      | Overflow status and interrupt disable bit that is set when counter overflows |
| MINH    | If set, then counting of events in M-mode is inhibited                       |
| SINH    | If set, then counting of events in S/HS-mode is inhibited                    |
| UINH    | If set, then counting of events in U-mode is inhibited                       |
| VSINH   | If set, then counting of events in VS-mode is inhibited                      |
| VUINH   | If set, then counting of events in VU-mode is inhibited                      |
| WPRI    | Reserved                                                                     |
| WPRI    | Reserved                                                                     |

For each x INH bit, if the associated privilege mode is not implemented, the bit is read-only zero.

Each of the five x INH bits, when set, inhibit counting of events while in privilege mode x .  All-zeroes for these bits results in counting of events in all modes.

The OF bit is set when the corresponding hpmcounter overflows, and remains set until written by software. Since hpmcounter  values  are  unsigned  values,  overflow is defined as unsigned  overflow  of  the implemented counter bits. Note that there is no loss of information after an overflow since the counter wraps around and keeps counting while the sticky OF bit remains set.

If supervisor mode is implemented, the 32-bit scountovf register contains read-only shadow copies of the OF bits in all 29 mhpmevent registers.

If an hpmcounter overflows while the associated OF bit is zero, then a "count overflow interrupt request" is generated.  If  the  OF  bit  is  one,  then  no  interrupt  request  is  generated.  Consequently  the  OF  bit  also functions as a count overflow interrupt disable for the associated hpmcounter.

Count  overflow  never  results  from  writes  to  the  mhpmcounter n or  mhpmevent n registers,  only  from hardware increments of counter registers.

This count-overflow-interrupt-request signal is treated as a standard local interrupt that corresponds to bit 13 in the mip / mie / sip / sie registers. The mip / sip LCOFIP and mie / sie LCOFIE bits are, respectively, the interrupt-pending and interrupt-enable bits for this interrupt. ('LCOFI' represents 'Local Count Overflow Interrupt'.)

Generation of a count-overflow-interrupt request by an hpmcounter sets the associated OF bit. When an OF bit is set, it eventually, but not necessarily immediately, sets the LCOFIP bit in the mip / sip registers. The LCOFIP bit is cleared by software before servicing the count overflow interrupt resulting from one or more count overflows. The mideleg register controls the delegation of this interrupt to S-mode versus M-mode.#

<image>

There are not separate overflow status and overflow interrupt enable bits. In practice, enabling overflow interrupt generation (by clearing the OF bit) is done in conjunction with initializing the  counter  to  a  starting  value.  Once  a  counter  has  overflowed,  it  and  the  OF  bit  must  be reinitialized before another overflow interrupt can be generated.

<image>

Software can distinguish newly overflowed counters (yet to be serviced by an overflow interrupt handler) from overflowed counters that have already been serviced or that are configured to not generate an interrupt on overflow, by maintaining a bit mask reflecting which counters are active and due to eventually overflow.
============================================================
=========
RESPONSE:
=========
============================================================
- The **OF** bit in the **mhpmevent10** register **is set when the corresponding mhpmcounter10 overflows**, and **remains set until written by software**.  
- **Overflow** for mhpmcounter10 is defined as **unsigned overflow of the implemented counter bits** (the counter wraps around and keeps counting while the sticky OF bit remains set).  
- **If an hpmcounter overflows while the associated OF bit is zero, then a "count overflow interrupt request" is generated**.  
- **If the OF bit is one, then no interrupt request is generated**.  
- **The OF bit also functions as a count overflow interrupt disable for mhpmcounter10**.  
- **Count overflow never results from writes to the mhpmcounter10 or mhpmevent10 registers, only from hardware increments of counter registers**.  

- For each **x INH** bit in **mhpmevent10** (where x ∈ {M, S, U, VS, VU}):  
  - **If set, then counting of events in privilege mode x is inhibited**.  
  - **If the associated privilege mode is not implemented, the bit is read‑only zero**.  
- **All‑zeroes for the five INH bits results in counting of events in all modes**.  

- **If supervisor mode is implemented, the 32‑bit scountovf register contains read‑only shadow copies of the OF bits in all 29 mhpmevent registers, including mhpmevent10**.  

- **Generation of a count‑overflow‑interrupt request by mhpmcounter10 sets the associated OF bit**.  

- **When an OF bit (including the one for mhpmcounter10) is set, it eventually, but not necessarily immediately, sets the LCOFIP bit in the mip/sip registers**.  

- **The LCOFIP bit is cleared by software before servicing the count overflow interrupt resulting from one or more count overflows**.  

- **The mip/sip LCOFIP and mie/sie LCOFIE bits are, respectively, the interrupt‑pending and interrupt‑enable bits for this interrupt** (bit 13 in the mip/mie/sip/sie registers).  

- **The mideleg register controls the delegation of this interrupt to S‑mode versus M‑mode**.  

- **There are not separate overflow status and overflow interrupt enable bits**.  

- **Enabling overflow interrupt generation (by clearing the OF bit) is done in conjunction with initializing mhpmcounter10 to a starting value**.  

- **Once mhpmcounter10 has overflowed, it and the OF bit must be reinitialized before another overflow interrupt can be generated**.  

- **Software can distinguish newly overflowed counters (yet to be serviced by an overflow interrupt handler) from overflowed counters that have already been serviced or that are configured to not generate an interrupt on overflow, by maintaining a bit mask reflecting which counters are active and due to eventually overflow** (applies to mhpmcounter10 as one of the counters).

## 3.1.10. Hardware Performance Monitor

M-mode includes a basic hardware performance-monitoring facility. The mcycle CSR counts the number of clock cycles executed by the processor core on which the hart is running. The minstret CSR counts the number of instructions the hart has retired. The mcycle and minstret registers have 64-bit precision on all RV32 and RV64 harts.

The counter registers have an arbitrary value after the hart is reset, and can be written with a given value. Any CSR write takes effect after the writing instruction has otherwise completed. The mcycle CSR may be shared between harts on the same core, in which case writes to mcycle will be visible to those harts. The platform should provide a mechanism to indicate which harts share an mcycle CSR.

The  hardware  performance  monitor  includes  29  additional  64-bit  event  counters, mhpmcounter3 -mhpmcounter31 . The event selector CSRs, mhpmevent3 -mhpmevent31 , are 64-bit WARL registers that control which event causes the corresponding counter to increment. The meaning of these events is defined by the platform,  but  event  0  is  defined  to  mean  "no  event."  All  counters  should  be  implemented,  but  a  legal implementation is to make both the counter and its corresponding event selector be read-only 0.

Figure 17. Hardware performance monitor counters.

<image>

The mhpmcounters are WARL registers that support up to 64 bits of precision on RV32 and RV64.

When XLEN=32, reads of the mcycle , minstret , mhpmcounter n , and mhpmevent n CSRs return bitj 31-0 of the corresponding register, and writes change only bits 31-0; reads of the mcycleh , minstreth , mhpmcounter n h , and mhpmevent n h CSRs return bits 63-32 of the corresponding register, and writes change only bits 63-32. The mhpmevent n h CSRs are provided only if the Sscofpmf extension is implemented.
============================================================

- After a hart reset, mhpmcounter11 has an arbitrary value.

- The event selector CSR that controls which event causes mhpmcounter11 to increment is mhpmevent11, which is a 64‑bit WARL register.  
- Event 0 in mhpmevent11 is defined to mean "no event".

## 3.1.11. Machine Counter-Enable ( mcounteren ) Register

The counter-enable mcounteren register is a 32-bit register that controls the availability of the hardware performance-monitoring counters to the next-lower privileged mode.

64

64

Figure 18. Counter-enable ( mcounteren ) register.

<image>

The settings in this register only control accessibility. The act of reading or writing this register does not affect the underlying counters, which continue to increment even when not accessible.

When the CY, TM, IR, or HPM n bit  in  the mcounteren register is clear, attempts to read the cycle , time , instret ,  or hpmcountern register  while  executing  in  S-mode  or  U-mode  will  cause  an  illegal-instruction exception.  When  one  of  these  bits  is  set,  access  to  the  corresponding  register  is  permitted  in  the  next implemented privilege mode (S-mode if implemented, otherwise U-mode).

<image>

The counter-enable bits support two common use cases with minimal hardware. For harts that do not need high-performance timers and counters, machine-mode software can trap accesses and  implement  all  features  in  software.  For  harts  that  need  high-performance  timers  and counters  but  are  not  concerned  with  obfuscating  the  underlying  hardware  counters,  the counters can be directly exposed to lower privilege modes.

In  addition,  when  the  TM  bit  in  the mcounteren register  is  clear,  attempts  to  access  the stimecmp or vstimecmp register  while  executing  in  a  mode  less  privileged  than  M  will  cause  an  illegal-instruction exception.  When  this  bit  is  set,  access  to  the stimecmp or vstimecmp register  is  permitted  in  S-mode  if implemented, and access to the vstimecmp register (via stimecmp ) is permitted in VS-mode if implemented and not otherwise prevented by the TM bit in hcounteren .

The cycle , instret ,  and hpmcountern CSRs are read-only shadows of mcycle , minstret ,  and mhpmcounter n ,  respectively. The time CSR is a read-only shadow of the memory-mapped mtime register. Analogously, when  XLEN=32,  the cycleh , instreth and hpmcounternh CSRs  are  read-only  shadows  of mcycleh , minstreth and mhpmcounternh , respectively. When XLEN=32, the timeh CSR is a read-only shadow of the upper 32 bits of the memory-mapped mtime register, while time shadows only the lower 32 bits of mtime .

<image>

Implementations can convert reads of the time and timeh CSRs into loads to the memorymapped mtime register, or emulate this functionality on behalf of less-privileged modes in Mmode software.

In harts with U-mode, the mcounteren must be implemented, but all fields are WARL and may be read-only zero,  indicating  reads  to  the  corresponding  counter  will  cause  an  illegal-instruction  exception  when executing in a less-privileged mode. In harts without U-mode, the mcounteren register should not exist.
============================================================

## 21.1. Count Overflow Control

The following bits are added to mhpmevent :

| 63   | 62   | 61   | 60   | 59    | 58    | 57   | 56   |
|------|------|------|------|-------|-------|------|------|
| OF   | MINH | SINH | UINH | VSINH | VUINH | WPRI | WPRI |

| Field   | Description                                                                  |
|---------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| OF      | Overflow status and interrupt disable bit that is set when counter overflows |
| MINH    | If set, then counting of events in M-mode is inhibited                       |
| SINH    | If set, then counting of events in S/HS-mode is inhibited                    |
| UINH    | If set, then counting of events in U-mode is inhibited                       |
| VSINH   | If set, then counting of events in VS-mode is inhibited                      |
| VUINH   | If set, then counting of events in VU-mode is inhibited                      |
| WPRI    | Reserved                                                                     |
| WPRI    | Reserved                                                                     |

For each x INH bit, if the associated privilege mode is not implemented, the bit is read-only zero.

Each of the five x INH bits, when set, inhibit counting of events while in privilege mode x .  All-zeroes for these bits results in counting of events in all modes.

The OF bit is set when the corresponding hpmcounter overflows, and remains set until written by software. Since hpmcounter  values  are  unsigned  values,  overflow is defined as unsigned  overflow  of  the implemented counter bits. Note that there is no loss of information after an overflow since the counter wraps around and keeps counting while the sticky OF bit remains set.

If supervisor mode is implemented, the 32-bit scountovf register contains read-only shadow copies of the OF bits in all 29 mhpmevent registers.

If an hpmcounter overflows while the associated OF bit is zero, then a "count overflow interrupt request" is generated.  If  the  OF  bit  is  one,  then  no  interrupt  request  is  generated.  Consequently  the  OF  bit  also functions as a count overflow interrupt disable for the associated hpmcounter.

Count  overflow  never  results  from  writes  to  the  mhpmcounter n or  mhpmevent n registers,  only  from hardware increments of counter registers.

This count-overflow-interrupt-request signal is treated as a standard local interrupt that corresponds to bit 13 in the mip / mie / sip / sie registers. The mip / sip LCOFIP and mie / sie LCOFIE bits are, respectively, the interrupt-pending and interrupt-enable bits for this interrupt. ('LCOFI' represents 'Local Count Overflow Interrupt'.)

Generation of a count-overflow-interrupt request by an hpmcounter sets the associated OF bit. When an OF bit is set, it eventually, but not necessarily immediately, sets the LCOFIP bit in the mip / sip registers. The LCOFIP bit is cleared by software before servicing the count overflow interrupt resulting from one or more count overflows. The mideleg register controls the delegation of this interrupt to S-mode versus M-mode.#

<image>

There are not separate overflow status and overflow interrupt enable bits. In practice, enabling overflow interrupt generation (by clearing the OF bit) is done in conjunction with initializing the  counter  to  a  starting  value.  Once  a  counter  has  overflowed,  it  and  the  OF  bit  must  be reinitialized before another overflow interrupt can be generated.

<image>

Software can distinguish newly overflowed counters (yet to be serviced by an overflow interrupt handler) from overflowed counters that have already been serviced or that are configured to not generate an interrupt on overflow, by maintaining a bit mask reflecting which counters are active and due to eventually overflow.
