=========
============================================================
- **Overflow status (OF) bit behavior for mhpmcounter11**  
  - *Source:* "The OF bit is set when the corresponding hpmcounter overflows, and remains set until written by software."  
  - *Effect:* When mhpmcounter11 overflows, its associated OF bit in the corresponding mhpmevent11 register becomes 1 and stays 1 until software writes the OF bit to 0.

- **Definition of overflow for mhpmcounter11**  
  - *Source:* "Since hpmcounter values are unsigned values, overflow is defined as unsigned overflow of the implemented counter bits."  
  - *Effect:* An overflow of mhpmcounter11 occurs when an unsigned increment causes the implemented counter bits to wrap around from their maximum value to zero.

- **Information retention after overflow of mhpmcounter11**  
  - *Source:* "Note that there is no loss of information after an overflow since the counter wraps around and keeps counting while the sticky OF bit remains set."  
  - *Effect:* After mhpmcounter11 overflows, the counter continues counting (wrapping) and the OF bit stays set, preserving the overflow indication.

- **Count‑overflow interrupt generation for mhpmcounter11**  
  - *Source:* "If an hpmcounter overflows while the associated OF bit is zero, then a 'count overflow interrupt request' is generated. If the OF bit is one, then no interrupt request is generated."  
  - *Effect:* If mhpmcounter11 overflows and its OF bit is 0, a count‑overflow interrupt request is generated; if the OF bit is already 1, no interrupt request is generated.

- **Interrupt‑disable function of the OF bit for mhpmcounter11**  
  - *Source:* "Consequently the OF bit also functions as a count overflow interrupt disable for the associated hpmcounter."  
  - *Effect:* Setting the OF bit in mhpmevent11 disables further count‑overflow interrupt requests from mhpmcounter11.

- **Source of count‑overflow‑interrupt request signal for mhpmcounter11**  
  - *Source:* "This count‑overflow‑interrupt‑request signal is treated as a standard local interrupt that corresponds to bit 13 in the mip / mie / sip / sie registers."  
  - *Effect:* An overflow of mhpmcounter11 that generates an interrupt sets bit 13 (LCOFIP) in the appropriate local‑interrupt pending register (mip for M‑mode, sip for S‑mode).

- **Pending‑interrupt (LCOFIP) handling for mhpmcounter11**  
  - *Source:* "When an OF bit is set, it eventually, but not necessarily immediately, sets the LCOFIP bit in the mip / sip registers. The LCOFIP bit is cleared by software before servicing the count overflow interrupt resulting from one or more count overflows."  
  - *Effect:* After mhpmcounter11's OF bit becomes 1, the LCOFIP bit will later be set; software must clear LCOFIP before handling the overflow interrupt.

- **Delegation of the count‑overflow interrupt generated by mhpmcounter11**  
  - *Source:* "The mideleg register controls the delegation of this interrupt to S-mode versus M-mode."  
  - *Effect:* Whether the overflow interrupt from mhpmcounter11 is taken in S‑mode or M‑mode is determined by the appropriate bit(s) in the mideleg register.

- **No overflow caused by software writes to mhpmcounter11**  
  - *Source:* "Count overflow never results from writes to the mhpmcounter n or mhpmevent n registers, only from hardware increments of counter registers."  
  - *Effect:* Writing to mhpmcounter11 or mhpmevent11 cannot cause an overflow; only hardware‑performed increments can.

- **Shadow copy of OF bit for mhpmcounter11 (if supervisor mode is implemented)**  
  - *Source:* "If supervisor mode is implemented, the 32‑bit scountovf register contains read‑only shadow copies of the OF bits in all 29 mhpmevent registers."  
  - *Effect:* When supervisor mode exists, bit 11 of scountovf reflects the OF bit of mhpmevent11 (read‑only).

- **INH bits that control counting for mhpmcounter11**  
  - *Source:* Table entries for mhpmevent bits: MINH, SINH, UINH, VSINH, VUINH, each described as "If set, then counting of events in … mode is inhibited."  
  - *Effect:* Setting MINH in mhpmevent11 inhibits counting of events for mhpmcounter11 while in M‑mode; setting SINH inhibits counting while in S/HS‑mode; setting UINH inhibits counting while in U‑mode; setting VSINH inhibits counting while in VS‑mode; setting VUINH inhibits counting while in VU‑mode. If all five bits are zero, counting proceeds in all modes.

- **Read‑only zero behavior of INH bits for unimplemented privilege modes (relevant to mhpmcounter11)**  
  - *Source:* "For each x INH bit, if the associated privilege mode is not implemented, the bit is read‑only zero."  
  - *Effect:* If a privilege mode (e.g., VU) is not implemented, the corresponding INH bit in mhpmevent11 reads as zero and cannot inhibit counting for that mode.

- **Requirement to re‑initialize mhpmcounter11 and its OF bit after an overflow**  
  - *Source:* "Once a counter has overflowed, it and the OF bit must be reinitialized before another overflow interrupt can be generated."  
  - *Effect:* After mhpmcounter11 overflows, software must write a new starting value to mhpmcounter11 and clear its OF bit before a subsequent overflow can cause another interrupt.

## 3.1.10. Hardware Performance Monitor

M-mode includes a basic hardware performance-monitoring facility. The mcycle CSR counts the number of clock cycles executed by the processor core on which the hart is running. The minstret CSR counts the number of instructions the hart has retired. The mcycle and minstret registers have 64-bit precision on all RV32 and RV64 harts.

The counter registers have an arbitrary value after the hart is reset, and can be written with a given value. Any CSR write takes effect after the writing instruction has otherwise completed. The mcycle CSR may be shared between harts on the same core, in which case writes to mcycle will be visible to those harts. The platform should provide a mechanism to indicate which harts share an mcycle CSR.

The  hardware  performance  monitor  includes  29  additional  64-bit  event  counters, mhpmcounter3 -mhpmcounter31 . The event selector CSRs, mhpmevent3 -mhpmevent31 , are 64-bit WARL registers that control which event causes the corresponding counter to increment. The meaning of these events is defined by the platform,  but  event  0  is  defined  to  mean  "no  event."  All  counters  should  be  implemented,  but  a  legal implementation is to make both the counter and its corresponding event selector be read-only 0.

Figure 17. Hardware performance monitor counters.

<image>

The mhpmcounters are WARL registers that support up to 64 bits of precision on RV32 and RV64.

When XLEN=32, reads of the mcycle , minstret , mhpmcounter n , and mhpmevent n CSRs return bitj 31-0 of the corresponding register, and writes change only bits 31-0; reads of the mcycleh , minstreth , mhpmcounter n h , and mhpmevent n h CSRs return bits 63-32 of the corresponding register, and writes change only bits 63-32. The mhpmevent n h CSRs are provided only if the Sscofpmf extension is implemented.

=========
============================================================
- The mhpmcounter12 CSR is one of the 29 additional 64‑bit event counters defined as **mhpmcounter3 – mhpmcounter31**.  
- The mhpmcounter12 CSR is a **WARL** register that **supports up to 64 bits of precision on RV32 and RV64**.  
- After a hart reset, the mhpmcounter12 register **has an arbitrary value**; it **may be written with a given value**.  
- **Any CSR write to mhpmcounter12 takes effect after the writing instruction has otherwise completed.**  
- When **XLEN = 32**:  
  - **Reads of mhpmcounter12 return bits 31‑0** of the corresponding register.  
  - **Writes to mhpmcounter12 change only bits 31‑0** of the register.  
  - The high‑half CSR **mhpmcounter12h** (if present) **returns bits 63‑32** on reads and **writes change only bits 63‑32**.  
- The **mhpmevent12** CSR (the event selector corresponding to mhpmcounter12) is a **64‑bit WARL register that controls which event causes mhpmcounter12 to increment**.  
- **Event 0 is defined to mean "no event."** Consequently, if **mhpmevent12 = 0**, mhpmcounter12 will not be incremented by any event.  
- **All counters, including mhpmcounter12, should be implemented, but a legal implementation may make both the counter and its corresponding event selector read‑only 0.**

## 3.1.11. Machine Counter-Enable ( mcounteren ) Register

The counter-enable mcounteren register is a 32-bit register that controls the availability of the hardware performance-monitoring counters to the next-lower privileged mode.

64

64

Figure 18. Counter-enable ( mcounteren ) register.

<image>

The settings in this register only control accessibility. The act of reading or writing this register does not affect the underlying counters, which continue to increment even when not accessible.

When the CY, TM, IR, or HPM n bit  in  the mcounteren register is clear, attempts to read the cycle , time , instret ,  or hpmcountern register  while  executing  in  S-mode  or  U-mode  will  cause  an  illegal-instruction exception.  When  one  of  these  bits  is  set,  access  to  the  corresponding  register  is  permitted  in  the  next implemented privilege mode (S-mode if implemented, otherwise U-mode).

<image>

The counter-enable bits support two common use cases with minimal hardware. For harts that do not need high-performance timers and counters, machine-mode software can trap accesses and  implement  all  features  in  software.  For  harts  that  need  high-performance  timers  and counters  but  are  not  concerned  with  obfuscating  the  underlying  hardware  counters,  the counters can be directly exposed to lower privilege modes.

In  addition,  when  the  TM  bit  in  the mcounteren register  is  clear,  attempts  to  access  the stimecmp or vstimecmp register  while  executing  in  a  mode  less  privileged  than  M  will  cause  an  illegal-instruction exception.  When  this  bit  is  set,  access  to  the stimecmp or vstimecmp register  is  permitted  in  S-mode  if implemented, and access to the vstimecmp register (via stimecmp ) is permitted in VS-mode if implemented and not otherwise prevented by the TM bit in hcounteren .

The cycle , instret ,  and hpmcountern CSRs are read-only shadows of mcycle , minstret ,  and mhpmcounter n ,  respectively. The time CSR is a read-only shadow of the memory-mapped mtime register. Analogously, when  XLEN=32,  the cycleh , instreth and hpmcounternh CSRs  are  read-only  shadows  of mcycleh , minstreth and mhpmcounternh , respectively. When XLEN=32, the timeh CSR is a read-only shadow of the upper 32 bits of the memory-mapped mtime register, while time shadows only the lower 32 bits of mtime .

<image>

Implementations can convert reads of the time and timeh CSRs into loads to the memorymapped mtime register, or emulate this functionality on behalf of less-privileged modes in Mmode software.

In harts with U-mode, the mcounteren must be implemented, but all fields are WARL and may be read-only zero,  indicating  reads  to  the  corresponding  counter  will  cause  an  illegal-instruction  exception  when executing in a less-privileged mode. In harts without U-mode, the mcounteren register should not exist.

## 3.1.12. Machine Counter-Inhibit ( mcountinhibit ) Register

Figure 19. Counter-inhibit mcountinhibit register

<image>

The counter-inhibit register mcountinhibit is a 32-bit WARL register that controls which of the hardware performance-monitoring  counters  increment.  The  settings  in  this  register  only  control  whether  the counters increment; their accessibility is not affected by the setting of this register.

When  the  CY,  IR,  or  HPM n bit  in  the mcountinhibit register  is clear,  the mcycle , minstret ,  or mhpmcountern register increments as usual. When the CY, IR, or HPM n bit is set, the corresponding counter does not increment.

The mcycle CSR may be shared between harts on the same core, in which case the mcountinhibit.CY field is also shared between those harts, and so writes to mcountinhibit.CY will be visible to those harts.

If the mcountinhibit register is not implemented, the implementation behaves as though the register were set to zero.

<image>

When  the mcycle and minstret counters  are  not  needed,  it  is  desirable  to  conditionally inhibit them to reduce energy consumption. Providing a single CSR to inhibit all counters also allows the counters to be atomically sampled.

Because the mtime counter can be shared between multiple cores, it cannot be inhibited with the mcountinhibit mechanism.

RESPONSE:
=========

- When the **HPM12** bit in the **mcountinhibit** register is **set**, the **mhpmcounter12** register **does not increment**.  
- The **settings** in the **mcountinhibit** register **only control whether the counters increment; their accessibility is not affected** by the setting of this register, so the **mhpmcounter12** register remains accessible regardless of the HPM12 bit value.  
- **If the mcountinhibit register is not implemented**, the implementation **behaves as though the register were set to zero**; consequently the **HPM12 bit is effectively clear** and the **mhpmcounter12** register **increments as usual**.

## 21.1. Count Overflow Control

The following bits are added to mhpmevent :

| 63   | 62   | 61   | 60   | 59    | 58    | 57   | 56   |
|------|------|------|------|-------|-------|------|------|
| OF   | MINH | SINH | UINH | VSINH | VUINH | WPRI | WPRI |

| Field   | Description                                                                  |
|---------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| OF      | Overflow status and interrupt disable bit that is set when counter overflows |
| MINH    | If set, then counting of events in M-mode is inhibited                       |
| SINH    | If set, then counting of events in S/HS-mode is inhibited                    |
| UINH    | If set, then counting of events in U-mode is inhibited                       |
| VSINH   | If set, then counting of events in VS-mode is inhibited                      |
| VUINH   | If set, then counting of events in VU-mode is inhibited                      |
| WPRI    | Reserved                                                                     |
| WPRI    | Reserved                                                                     |

For each x INH bit, if the associated privilege mode is not implemented, the bit is read-only zero.

Each of the five x INH bits, when set, inhibit counting of events while in privilege mode x .  All-zeroes for these bits results in counting of events in all modes.

The OF bit is set when the corresponding hpmcounter overflows, and remains set until written by software. Since hpmcounter  values  are  unsigned  values,  overflow is defined as unsigned  overflow  of  the implemented counter bits. Note that there is no loss of information after an overflow since the counter wraps around and keeps counting while the sticky OF bit remains set.

If supervisor mode is implemented, the 32-bit scountovf register contains read-only shadow copies of the OF bits in all 29 mhpmevent registers.

If an hpmcounter overflows while the associated OF bit is zero, then a "count overflow interrupt request" is generated.  If  the  OF  bit  is  one,  then  no  interrupt  request  is  generated.  Consequently  the  OF  bit  also functions as a count overflow interrupt disable for the associated hpmcounter.

Count  overflow  never  results  from  writes  to  the  mhpmcounter n or  mhpmevent n registers,  only  from hardware increments of counter registers.

This count-overflow-interrupt-request signal is treated as a standard local interrupt that corresponds to bit 13 in the mip / mie / sip / sie registers. The mip / sip LCOFIP and mie / sie LCOFIE bits are, respectively, the interrupt-pending and interrupt-enable bits for this interrupt. ('LCOFI' represents 'Local Count Overflow Interrupt'.)

Generation of a count-overflow-interrupt request by an hpmcounter sets the associated OF bit. When an OF bit is set, it eventually, but not necessarily immediately, sets the LCOFIP bit in the mip / sip registers. The LCOFIP bit is cleared by software before servicing the count overflow interrupt resulting from one or more count overflows. The mideleg register controls the delegation of this interrupt to S-mode versus M-mode.#

<image>

There are not separate overflow status and overflow interrupt enable bits. In practice, enabling overflow interrupt generation (by clearing the OF bit) is done in conjunction with initializing the  counter  to  a  starting  value.  Once  a  counter  has  overflowed,  it  and  the  OF  bit  must  be reinitialized before another overflow interrupt can be generated.

<image>

Software can distinguish newly overflowed counters (yet to be serviced by an overflow interrupt handler) from overflowed counters that have already been serviced or that are configured to not generate an interrupt on overflow, by maintaining a bit mask reflecting which counters are active and due to eventually overflow.

## 3.1.10. Hardware Performance Monitor

M-mode includes a basic hardware performance-monitoring facility. The mcycle CSR counts the number of clock cycles executed by the processor core on which the hart is running. The minstret CSR counts the number of instructions the hart has retired. The mcycle and minstret registers have 64-bit precision on all RV32 and RV64 harts.

The counter registers have an arbitrary value after the hart is reset, and can be written with a given value. Any CSR write takes effect after the writing instruction has otherwise completed. The mcycle CSR may be shared between harts on the same core, in which case writes to mcycle will be visible to those harts. The platform should provide a mechanism to indicate which harts share an mcycle CSR.

The  hardware  performance  monitor  includes  29  additional  64-bit  event  counters, mhpmcounter3 -mhpmcounter31 . The event selector CSRs, mhpmevent3 -mhpmevent31 , are 64-bit WARL registers that control which event causes the corresponding counter to increment. The meaning of these events is defined by the platform,  but  event  0  is  defined  to  mean  "no  event."  All  counters  should  be  implemented,  but  a  legal implementation is to make both the counter and its corresponding event selector be read-only 0.

Figure 17. Hardware performance monitor counters.

<image>

The mhpmcounters are WARL registers that support up to 64 bits of precision on RV32 and RV64.

When XLEN=32, reads of the mcycle , minstret , mhpmcounter n , and mhpmevent n CSRs return bitj 31-0 of the corresponding register, and writes change only bits 31-0; reads of the mcycleh , minstreth , mhpmcounter n h , and mhpmevent n h CSRs return bits 63-32 of the corresponding register, and writes change only bits 63-32. The mhpmevent n h CSRs are provided only if the Sscofpmf extension is implemented.

- mhpmcounter13 is a WARL register that supports up to 64 bits of precision on RV32 and RV64.  

- The mhpmcounter13 register has an arbitrary value after the hart is reset, and can be written with a given value.  

- Any CSR write to mhpmcounter13 takes effect after the writing instruction has otherwise completed.  

- The event selector CSR mhpmevent13 is a 64‑bit WARL register that controls which event causes mhpmcounter13 to increment.  

- Event 0 is defined to mean "no event."  

- All counters should be implemented, but a legal implementation is to make both the counter (mhpmcounter13) and its corresponding event selector (mhpmevent13) be read‑only 0.  

- When XLEN=32, reads of the mhpmcounter13 CSR return bits 31‑0 of the corresponding register, and writes change only bits 31‑0.  

- When XLEN=32, reads of the mhpmcounter13h CSR return bits 63‑32 of the corresponding register, and writes change only bits 63‑32.

## 3.1.11. Machine Counter-Enable ( mcounteren ) Register

The counter-enable mcounteren register is a 32-bit register that controls the availability of the hardware performance-monitoring counters to the next-lower privileged mode.

64

64

Figure 18. Counter-enable ( mcounteren ) register.

<image>

The settings in this register only control accessibility. The act of reading or writing this register does not affect the underlying counters, which continue to increment even when not accessible.

When the CY, TM, IR, or HPM n bit  in  the mcounteren register is clear, attempts to read the cycle , time , instret ,  or hpmcountern register  while  executing  in  S-mode  or  U-mode  will  cause  an  illegal-instruction exception.  When  one  of  these  bits  is  set,  access  to  the  corresponding  register  is  permitted  in  the  next implemented privilege mode (S-mode if implemented, otherwise U-mode).

<image>

The counter-enable bits support two common use cases with minimal hardware. For harts that do not need high-performance timers and counters, machine-mode software can trap accesses and  implement  all  features  in  software.  For  harts  that  need  high-performance  timers  and counters  but  are  not  concerned  with  obfuscating  the  underlying  hardware  counters,  the counters can be directly exposed to lower privilege modes.

In  addition,  when  the  TM  bit  in  the mcounteren register  is  clear,  attempts  to  access  the stimecmp or vstimecmp register  while  executing  in  a  mode  less  privileged  than  M  will  cause  an  illegal-instruction exception.  When  this  bit  is  set,  access  to  the stimecmp or vstimecmp register  is  permitted  in  S-mode  if implemented, and access to the vstimecmp register (via stimecmp ) is permitted in VS-mode if implemented and not otherwise prevented by the TM bit in hcounteren .

The cycle , instret ,  and hpmcountern CSRs are read-only shadows of mcycle , minstret ,  and mhpmcounter n ,  respectively. The time CSR is a read-only shadow of the memory-mapped mtime register. Analogously, when  XLEN=32,  the cycleh , instreth and hpmcounternh CSRs  are  read-only  shadows  of mcycleh , minstreth and mhpmcounternh , respectively. When XLEN=32, the timeh CSR is a read-only shadow of the upper 32 bits of the memory-mapped mtime register, while time shadows only the lower 32 bits of mtime .

<image>

Implementations can convert reads of the time and timeh CSRs into loads to the memorymapped mtime register, or emulate this functionality on behalf of less-privileged modes in Mmode software.

In harts with U-mode, the mcounteren must be implemented, but all fields are WARL and may be read-only zero,  indicating  reads  to  the  corresponding  counter  will  cause  an  illegal-instruction  exception  when executing in a less-privileged mode. In harts without U-mode, the mcounteren register should not exist.

## 3.1.12. Machine Counter-Inhibit ( mcountinhibit ) Register

Figure 19. Counter-inhibit mcountinhibit register

<image>

The counter-inhibit register mcountinhibit is a 32-bit WARL register that controls which of the hardware performance-monitoring  counters  increment.  The  settings  in  this  register  only  control  whether  the counters increment; their accessibility is not affected by the setting of this register.

When  the  CY,  IR,  or  HPM n bit  in  the mcountinhibit register  is clear,  the mcycle , minstret ,  or mhpmcountern register increments as usual. When the CY, IR, or HPM n bit is set, the corresponding counter does not increment.

The mcycle CSR may be shared between harts on the same core, in which case the mcountinhibit.CY field is also shared between those harts, and so writes to mcountinhibit.CY will be visible to those harts.

If the mcountinhibit register is not implemented, the implementation behaves as though the register were set to zero.

<image>

When  the mcycle and minstret counters  are  not  needed,  it  is  desirable  to  conditionally inhibit them to reduce energy consumption. Providing a single CSR to inhibit all counters also allows the counters to be atomically sampled.

Because the mtime counter can be shared between multiple cores, it cannot be inhibited with the mcountinhibit mechanism.

=========

=========

- When the HPM13 bit in the mcountinhibit register is **clear**, the mhpmcounter13 register **increments as usual**.  

- When the HPM13 bit in the mcountinhibit register is **set**, the mhpmcounter13 register **does not increment**.  

- The settings in the mcountinhibit register **only control whether the counters increment; their accessibility is not affected**.  

- If the mcountinhibit register is **not implemented**, the implementation **behaves as though the register were set to zero** (thereby the HPM13 bit is clear and mhpmcounter13 increments as usual).

## 5.2. Machine-level CSRs

| Number   | Privilege   | Width   | Name     | Description                       |
|----------|-------------|---------|----------|-----------------------------------|
| 0x350    | MRW         | XLEN    | miselect | Machine indirect register select  |
| 0x351    | MRW         | XLEN    | mireg    | Machine indirect register alias   |
| 0x352    | MRW         | XLEN    | mireg2   | Machine indirect register alias 2 |
| 0x353    | MRW         | XLEN    | mireg3   | Machine indirect register alias 3 |
| 0x355    | MRW         | XLEN    | mireg4   | Machine indirect register alias 4 |
| 0x356    | MRW         | XLEN    | mireg5   | Machine indirect register alias 5 |
| 0x357    | MRW         | XLEN    | mireg6   | Machine indirect register alias 6 |

<image>

The mireg* CSR numbers are not consecutive because miph is CSR number 0x354.

The CSRs listed in the table above provide a window for accessing register state indirectly. The value of miselect determines which register is accessed upon read or write of each of the machine indirect alias CSRs ( mireg* ). miselect value  ranges  are  allocated  to  dependent  extensions,  which  specify  the  register state accessible via each mireg i register, for each miselect value. miselect is a WARL register.

The miselect register  implements  at  least  enough  bits  to  support  all  implemented miselect values (corresponding to the implemented extensions that utilize miselect / mireg* to  indirectly  access  register state). The miselect register may be read-only zero if there are no extensions implemented that utilize it.

Values of miselect with the most-significant bit set (bit XLEN - 1 = 1) are designated only for custom use, presumably  for  accessing  custom  registers  through  the  alias  CSRs.  Values  of miselect with  the  mostsignificant  bit  clear  are  designated  only  for  standard  use  and  are  reserved  until  allocated  to  a  standard architecture extension. If XLEN is changed, the most-significant bit of miselect moves to the new position, retaining its value from before.

<image>

An implementation is not required to support any custom values for miselect .

The behavior upon accessing mireg* from M-mode, while miselect holds a value that is not implemented, is UNSPECIFIED.

<image>

It is expected that implementations will typically raise an illegal-instruction exception for such accesses, so that, for example, they can be identified as software bugs. Platform specs, profile specs,  and/or  the  Privileged  ISA  spec  may  place  more  restrictions  on  behavior  for  such accesses.

Attempts to access mireg* while miselect holds a number in an allocated and implemented range results in a specific behavior that, for each combination of miselect and mireg i ,  is  defined by the extension to which the miselect value is allocated.

Ordinarily, each mireg i will access register state, access read-only 0 state, or raise an illegalinstruction exception.

<image>

<image>

For  RV32,  if  an  extension  defines  an  indirectly  accessed  register  as  64  bits  wide,  it  is recommended that the lower 32 bits of the register are accessed through one of mireg , mireg2 , or mireg3 ,  while  the  upper  32  bits  are  accessed  through mireg4 , mireg5 ,  or mireg6 , respectively.

Six *ireg* registers are defined in order to ensure that the needs of extensions in development are covered, with some room for growth. For example, for an siselect value associated with counter X, sireg / sireg2 could be used to access mhpmcounterX / mhpmeventX ,  while sireg4 / sireg5 could access mhpmcounterXh / mhpmeventXh . Six *ireg* registers allows for accessing up to  3  CSR  arrays  per  index  ( *iselect )  with  RV32-only  CSRs,  or  up  to  6  CSR  arrays  per index value without RV32-only CSRs.

## 21.1. Count Overflow Control

The following bits are added to mhpmevent :

| 63   | 62   | 61   | 60   | 59    | 58    | 57   | 56   |
|------|------|------|------|-------|-------|------|------|
| OF   | MINH | SINH | UINH | VSINH | VUINH | WPRI | WPRI |

| Field   | Description                                                                  |
|---------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| OF      | Overflow status and interrupt disable bit that is set when counter overflows |
| MINH    | If set, then counting of events in M-mode is inhibited                       |
| SINH    | If set, then counting of events in S/HS-mode is inhibited                    |
| UINH    | If set, then counting of events in U-mode is inhibited                       |
| VSINH   | If set, then counting of events in VS-mode is inhibited                      |
| VUINH   | If set, then counting of events in VU-mode is inhibited                      |
| WPRI    | Reserved                                                                     |
| WPRI    | Reserved                                                                     |

For each x INH bit, if the associated privilege mode is not implemented, the bit is read-only zero.

Each of the five x INH bits, when set, inhibit counting of events while in privilege mode x .  All-zeroes for these bits results in counting of events in all modes.

The OF bit is set when the corresponding hpmcounter overflows, and remains set until written by software. Since hpmcounter  values  are  unsigned  values,  overflow is defined as unsigned  overflow  of  the implemented counter bits. Note that there is no loss of information after an overflow since the counter wraps around and keeps counting while the sticky OF bit remains set.

If supervisor mode is implemented, the 32-bit scountovf register contains read-only shadow copies of the OF bits in all 29 mhpmevent registers.

If an hpmcounter overflows while the associated OF bit is zero, then a "count overflow interrupt request" is generated.  If  the  OF  bit  is  one,  then  no  interrupt  request  is  generated.  Consequently  the  OF  bit  also functions as a count overflow interrupt disable for the associated hpmcounter.

Count  overflow  never  results  from  writes  to  the  mhpmcounter n or  mhpmevent n registers,  only  from hardware increments of counter registers.

This count-overflow-interrupt-request signal is treated as a standard local interrupt that corresponds to bit 13 in the mip / mie / sip / sie registers. The mip / sip LCOFIP and mie / sie LCOFIE bits are, respectively, the interrupt-pending and interrupt-enable bits for this interrupt. ('LCOFI' represents 'Local Count Overflow Interrupt'.)

Generation of a count-overflow-interrupt request by an hpmcounter sets the associated OF bit. When an OF bit is set, it eventually, but not necessarily immediately, sets the LCOFIP bit in the mip / sip registers. The LCOFIP bit is cleared by software before servicing the count overflow interrupt resulting from one or more count overflows. The mideleg register controls the delegation of this interrupt to S-mode versus M-mode.#

<image>

There are not separate overflow status and overflow interrupt enable bits. In practice, enabling overflow interrupt generation (by clearing the OF bit) is done in conjunction with initializing the  counter  to  a  starting  value.  Once  a  counter  has  overflowed,  it  and  the  OF  bit  must  be reinitialized before another overflow interrupt can be generated.

<image>

Software can distinguish newly overflowed counters (yet to be serviced by an overflow interrupt handler) from overflowed counters that have already been serviced or that are configured to not generate an interrupt on overflow, by maintaining a bit mask reflecting which counters are active and due to eventually overflow.

- For each *x INH* bit in mhpmevent13, **if the associated privilege mode is not implemented, the bit is read‑only zero**.  

- **Each of the five x INH bits, when set, inhibit counting of events while in privilege mode x**. **All‑zeroes for these bits results in counting of events in all modes**.  

- **The OF bit in mhpmevent13 is set when the corresponding mhpmcounter13 overflows, and remains set until written by software**. **Since hpmcounter values are unsigned values, overflow is defined as unsigned overflow of the implemented counter bits**.

- **If supervisor mode is implemented, the 32‑bit scountovf register contains read‑only shadow copies of the OF bits in all 29 mhpmevent registers**, therefore **scountovf bit 13 reflects the OF bit of mhpmevent13**.  

- **If an hpmcounter overflows while the associated OF bit is zero, then a "count overflow interrupt request" is generated**. **If the OF bit is one, then no interrupt request is generated**. **Consequently the OF bit also functions as a count overflow interrupt disable for the associated hpmcounter13**.

## 3.1.10. Hardware Performance Monitor

M-mode includes a basic hardware performance-monitoring facility. The mcycle CSR counts the number of clock cycles executed by the processor core on which the hart is running. The minstret CSR counts the number of instructions the hart has retired. The mcycle and minstret registers have 64-bit precision on all RV32 and RV64 harts.

The counter registers have an arbitrary value after the hart is reset, and can be written with a given value. Any CSR write takes effect after the writing instruction has otherwise completed. The mcycle CSR may be shared between harts on the same core, in which case writes to mcycle will be visible to those harts. The platform should provide a mechanism to indicate which harts share an mcycle CSR.

The  hardware  performance  monitor  includes  29  additional  64-bit  event  counters, mhpmcounter3 -mhpmcounter31 . The event selector CSRs, mhpmevent3 -mhpmevent31 , are 64-bit WARL registers that control which event causes the corresponding counter to increment. The meaning of these events is defined by the platform,  but  event  0  is  defined  to  mean  "no  event."  All  counters  should  be  implemented,  but  a  legal implementation is to make both the counter and its corresponding event selector be read-only 0.

Figure 17. Hardware performance monitor counters.

<image>

The mhpmcounters are WARL registers that support up to 64 bits of precision on RV32 and RV64.

When XLEN=32, reads of the mcycle , minstret , mhpmcounter n , and mhpmevent n CSRs return bitj 31-0 of the corresponding register, and writes change only bits 31-0; reads of the mcycleh , minstreth , mhpmcounter n h , and mhpmevent n h CSRs return bits 63-32 of the corresponding register, and writes change only bits 63-32. The mhpmevent n h CSRs are provided only if the Sscofpmf extension is implemented.
============================================================
=========

=========

- The mhpmcounters are WARL registers that support up to 64 bits of precision on RV32 and RV64.  

- The counter registers have an arbitrary value after the hart is reset, and can be written with a given value. Any CSR write takes effect after the writing instruction has otherwise completed.  

- The event selector CSR, mhpmevent14, is a 64‑bit WARL register that controls which event causes the corresponding counter to increment. The meaning of these events is defined by the platform, but event 0 is defined to mean "no event."

## 3.1.11. Machine Counter-Enable ( mcounteren ) Register

The counter-enable mcounteren register is a 32-bit register that controls the availability of the hardware performance-monitoring counters to the next-lower privileged mode.

64

64

Figure 18. Counter-enable ( mcounteren ) register.

<image>

The settings in this register only control accessibility. The act of reading or writing this register does not affect the underlying counters, which continue to increment even when not accessible.

When the CY, TM, IR, or HPM n bit  in  the mcounteren register is clear, attempts to read the cycle , time , instret ,  or hpmcountern register  while  executing  in  S-mode  or  U-mode  will  cause  an  illegal-instruction exception.  When  one  of  these  bits  is  set,  access  to  the  corresponding  register  is  permitted  in  the  next implemented privilege mode (S-mode if implemented, otherwise U-mode).

<image>

The counter-enable bits support two common use cases with minimal hardware. For harts that do not need high-performance timers and counters, machine-mode software can trap accesses and  implement  all  features  in  software.  For  harts  that  need  high-performance  timers  and counters  but  are  not  concerned  with  obfuscating  the  underlying  hardware  counters,  the counters can be directly exposed to lower privilege modes.

In  addition,  when  the  TM  bit  in  the mcounteren register  is  clear,  attempts  to  access  the stimecmp or vstimecmp register  while  executing  in  a  mode  less  privileged  than  M  will  cause  an  illegal-instruction exception.  When  this  bit  is  set,  access  to  the stimecmp or vstimecmp register  is  permitted  in  S-mode  if implemented, and access to the vstimecmp register (via stimecmp ) is permitted in VS-mode if implemented and not otherwise prevented by the TM bit in hcounteren .

The cycle , instret ,  and hpmcountern CSRs are read-only shadows of mcycle , minstret ,  and mhpmcounter n ,  respectively. The time CSR is a read-only shadow of the memory-mapped mtime register. Analogously, when  XLEN=32,  the cycleh , instreth and hpmcounternh CSRs  are  read-only  shadows  of mcycleh , minstreth and mhpmcounternh , respectively. When XLEN=32, the timeh CSR is a read-only shadow of the upper 32 bits of the memory-mapped mtime register, while time shadows only the lower 32 bits of mtime .

<image>

Implementations can convert reads of the time and timeh CSRs into loads to the memorymapped mtime register, or emulate this functionality on behalf of less-privileged modes in Mmode software.

In harts with U-mode, the mcounteren must be implemented, but all fields are WARL and may be read-only zero,  indicating  reads  to  the  corresponding  counter  will  cause  an  illegal-instruction  exception  when executing in a less-privileged mode. In harts without U-mode, the mcounteren register should not exist.

## 3.1.12. Machine Counter-Inhibit ( mcountinhibit ) Register

Figure 19. Counter-inhibit mcountinhibit register

<image>

The counter-inhibit register mcountinhibit is a 32-bit WARL register that controls which of the hardware performance-monitoring  counters  increment.  The  settings  in  this  register  only  control  whether  the counters increment; their accessibility is not affected by the setting of this register.

When  the  CY,  IR,  or  HPM n bit  in  the mcountinhibit register  is clear,  the mcycle , minstret ,  or mhpmcountern register increments as usual. When the CY, IR, or HPM n bit is set, the corresponding counter does not increment.

The mcycle CSR may be shared between harts on the same core, in which case the mcountinhibit.CY field is also shared between those harts, and so writes to mcountinhibit.CY will be visible to those harts.

If the mcountinhibit register is not implemented, the implementation behaves as though the register were set to zero.

<image>

When  the mcycle and minstret counters  are  not  needed,  it  is  desirable  to  conditionally inhibit them to reduce energy consumption. Providing a single CSR to inhibit all counters also allows the counters to be atomically sampled.

Because the mtime counter can be shared between multiple cores, it cannot be inhibited with the mcountinhibit mechanism.
============================================================
=========
RESPONSE:
=========
============================================================

## 21.1. Count Overflow Control

The following bits are added to mhpmevent :

| 63   | 62   | 61   | 60   | 59    | 58    | 57   | 56   |
|------|------|------|------|-------|-------|------|------|
| OF   | MINH | SINH | UINH | VSINH | VUINH | WPRI | WPRI |

| Field   | Description                                                                  |
|---------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| OF      | Overflow status and interrupt disable bit that is set when counter overflows |
| MINH    | If set, then counting of events in M-mode is inhibited                       |
| SINH    | If set, then counting of events in S/HS-mode is inhibited                    |
| UINH    | If set, then counting of events in U-mode is inhibited                       |
| VSINH   | If set, then counting of events in VS-mode is inhibited                      |
| VUINH   | If set, then counting of events in VU-mode is inhibited                      |
| WPRI    | Reserved                                                                     |
| WPRI    | Reserved                                                                     |

For each x INH bit, if the associated privilege mode is not implemented, the bit is read-only zero.

Each of the five x INH bits, when set, inhibit counting of events while in privilege mode x .  All-zeroes for these bits results in counting of events in all modes.

The OF bit is set when the corresponding hpmcounter overflows, and remains set until written by software. Since hpmcounter  values  are  unsigned  values,  overflow is defined as unsigned  overflow  of  the implemented counter bits. Note that there is no loss of information after an overflow since the counter wraps around and keeps counting while the sticky OF bit remains set.

If supervisor mode is implemented, the 32-bit scountovf register contains read-only shadow copies of the OF bits in all 29 mhpmevent registers.

If an hpmcounter overflows while the associated OF bit is zero, then a "count overflow interrupt request" is generated.  If  the  OF  bit  is  one,  then  no  interrupt  request  is  generated.  Consequently  the  OF  bit  also functions as a count overflow interrupt disable for the associated hpmcounter.

Count  overflow  never  results  from  writes  to  the  mhpmcounter n or  mhpmevent n registers,  only  from hardware increments of counter registers.

This count-overflow-interrupt-request signal is treated as a standard local interrupt that corresponds to bit 13 in the mip / mie / sip / sie registers. The mip / sip LCOFIP and mie / sie LCOFIE bits are, respectively, the interrupt-pending and interrupt-enable bits for this interrupt. ('LCOFI' represents 'Local Count Overflow Interrupt'.)

Generation of a count-overflow-interrupt request by an hpmcounter sets the associated OF bit. When an OF bit is set, it eventually, but not necessarily immediately, sets the LCOFIP bit in the mip / sip registers. The LCOFIP bit is cleared by software before servicing the count overflow interrupt resulting from one or more count overflows. The mideleg register controls the delegation of this interrupt to S-mode versus M-mode.#

<image>

There are not separate overflow status and overflow interrupt enable bits. In practice, enabling overflow interrupt generation (by clearing the OF bit) is done in conjunction with initializing the  counter  to  a  starting  value.  Once  a  counter  has  overflowed,  it  and  the  OF  bit  must  be reinitialized before another overflow interrupt can be generated.

<image>

Software can distinguish newly overflowed counters (yet to be serviced by an overflow interrupt handler) from overflowed counters that have already been serviced or that are configured to not generate an interrupt on overflow, by maintaining a bit mask reflecting which counters are active and due to eventually overflow.

## 3.1.10. Hardware Performance Monitor

M-mode includes a basic hardware performance-monitoring facility. The mcycle CSR counts the number of clock cycles executed by the processor core on which the hart is running. The minstret CSR counts the number of instructions the hart has retired. The mcycle and minstret registers have 64-bit precision on all RV32 and RV64 harts.

The counter registers have an arbitrary value after the hart is reset, and can be written with a given value. Any CSR write takes effect after the writing instruction has otherwise completed. The mcycle CSR may be shared between harts on the same core, in which case writes to mcycle will be visible to those harts. The platform should provide a mechanism to indicate which harts share an mcycle CSR.

The  hardware  performance  monitor  includes  29  additional  64-bit  event  counters, mhpmcounter3 -mhpmcounter31 . The event selector CSRs, mhpmevent3 -mhpmevent31 , are 64-bit WARL registers that control which event causes the corresponding counter to increment. The meaning of these events is defined by the platform,  but  event  0  is  defined  to  mean  "no  event."  All  counters  should  be  implemented,  but  a  legal implementation is to make both the counter and its corresponding event selector be read-only 0.

Figure 17. Hardware performance monitor counters.

<image>

The mhpmcounters are WARL registers that support up to 64 bits of precision on RV32 and RV64.

When XLEN=32, reads of the mcycle , minstret , mhpmcounter n , and mhpmevent n CSRs return bitj 31-0 of the corresponding register, and writes change only bits 31-0; reads of the mcycleh , minstreth , mhpmcounter n h , and mhpmevent n h CSRs return bits 63-32 of the corresponding register, and writes change only bits 63-32. The mhpmevent n h CSRs are provided only if the Sscofpmf extension is implemented.

## 3.1.11. Machine Counter-Enable ( mcounteren ) Register

The counter-enable mcounteren register is a 32-bit register that controls the availability of the hardware performance-monitoring counters to the next-lower privileged mode.

64

64

Figure 18. Counter-enable ( mcounteren ) register.

<image>

The settings in this register only control accessibility. The act of reading or writing this register does not affect the underlying counters, which continue to increment even when not accessible.

When the CY, TM, IR, or HPM n bit  in  the mcounteren register is clear, attempts to read the cycle , time , instret ,  or hpmcountern register  while  executing  in  S-mode  or  U-mode  will  cause  an  illegal-instruction exception.  When  one  of  these  bits  is  set,  access  to  the  corresponding  register  is  permitted  in  the  next implemented privilege mode (S-mode if implemented, otherwise U-mode).

<image>

The counter-enable bits support two common use cases with minimal hardware. For harts that do not need high-performance timers and counters, machine-mode software can trap accesses and  implement  all  features  in  software.  For  harts  that  need  high-performance  timers  and counters  but  are  not  concerned  with  obfuscating  the  underlying  hardware  counters,  the counters can be directly exposed to lower privilege modes.

In  addition,  when  the  TM  bit  in  the mcounteren register  is  clear,  attempts  to  access  the stimecmp or vstimecmp register  while  executing  in  a  mode  less  privileged  than  M  will  cause  an  illegal-instruction exception.  When  this  bit  is  set,  access  to  the stimecmp or vstimecmp register  is  permitted  in  S-mode  if implemented, and access to the vstimecmp register (via stimecmp ) is permitted in VS-mode if implemented and not otherwise prevented by the TM bit in hcounteren .

The cycle , instret ,  and hpmcountern CSRs are read-only shadows of mcycle , minstret ,  and mhpmcounter n ,  respectively. The time CSR is a read-only shadow of the memory-mapped mtime register. Analogously, when  XLEN=32,  the cycleh , instreth and hpmcounternh CSRs  are  read-only  shadows  of mcycleh , minstreth and mhpmcounternh , respectively. When XLEN=32, the timeh CSR is a read-only shadow of the upper 32 bits of the memory-mapped mtime register, while time shadows only the lower 32 bits of mtime .

<image>

Implementations can convert reads of the time and timeh CSRs into loads to the memorymapped mtime register, or emulate this functionality on behalf of less-privileged modes in Mmode software.

In harts with U-mode, the mcounteren must be implemented, but all fields are WARL and may be read-only zero,  indicating  reads  to  the  corresponding  counter  will  cause  an  illegal-instruction  exception  when executing in a less-privileged mode. In harts without U-mode, the mcounteren register should not exist.

| SINH    | If set, then counting of events in S/HS-mode is inhibited                    |
| UINH    | If set, then counting of events in U-mode is inhibited                       |
| VSINH   | If set, then counting of events in VS-mode is inhibited                      |
| VUINH   | If set, then counting of events in VU-mode is inhibited                      |
| WPRI    | Reserved                                                                     |
| WPRI    | Reserved                                                                     |

For each x INH bit, if the associated privilege mode is not implemented, the bit is read-only zero.

Each of the five x INH bits, when set, inhibit counting of events while in privilege mode x .  All-zeroes for these bits results in counting of events in all modes.

The OF bit is set when the corresponding hpmcounter overflows, and remains set until written by software. Since hpmcounter  values  are  unsigned  values,  overflow is defined as unsigned  overflow  of  the implemented counter bits. Note that there is no loss of information after an overflow since the counter wraps around and keeps counting while the sticky OF bit remains set.

If supervisor mode is implemented, the 32-bit scountovf register contains read-only shadow copies of the OF bits in all 29 mhpmevent registers.

If an hpmcounter overflows while the associated OF bit is zero, then a "count overflow interrupt request" is generated.  If  the  OF  bit  is  one,  then  no  interrupt  request  is  generated.  Consequently  the  OF  bit  also functions as a count overflow interrupt disable for the associated hpmcounter.

Count  overflow  never  results  from  writes  to  the  mhpmcounter n or  mhpmevent n registers,  only  from hardware increments of counter registers.

This count-overflow-interrupt-request signal is treated as a standard local interrupt that corresponds to bit 13 in the mip / mie / sip / sie registers. The mip / sip LCOFIP and mie / sie LCOFIE bits are, respectively, the interrupt-pending and interrupt-enable bits for this interrupt. ('LCOFI' represents 'Local Count Overflow Interrupt'.)

Generation of a count-overflow-interrupt request by an hpmcounter sets the associated OF bit. When an OF bit is set, it eventually, but not necessarily immediately, sets the LCOFIP bit in the mip / sip registers. The LCOFIP bit is cleared by software before servicing the count overflow interrupt resulting from one or more count overflows. The mideleg register controls the delegation of this interrupt to S-mode versus M-mode.#

<image>

There are not separate overflow status and overflow interrupt enable bits. In practice, enabling overflow interrupt generation (by clearing the OF bit) is done in conjunction with initializing the  counter  to  a  starting  value.  Once  a  counter  has  overflowed,  it  and  the  OF  bit  must  be reinitialized before another overflow interrupt can be generated.

<image>

Software can distinguish newly overflowed counters (yet to be serviced by an overflow interrupt handler) from overflowed counters that have already been serviced or that are configured to not generate an interrupt on overflow, by maintaining a bit mask reflecting which counters are active and due to eventually overflow.

## 3.1.10. Hardware Performance Monitor

M-mode includes a basic hardware performance-monitoring facility. The mcycle CSR counts the number of clock cycles executed by the processor core on which the hart is running. The minstret CSR counts the number of instructions the hart has retired. The mcycle and minstret registers have 64-bit precision on all RV32 and RV64 harts.

The counter registers have an arbitrary value after the hart is reset, and can be written with a given value. Any CSR write takes effect after the writing instruction has otherwise completed. The mcycle CSR may be shared between harts on the same core, in which case writes to mcycle will be visible to those harts. The platform should provide a mechanism to indicate which harts share an mcycle CSR.

The  hardware  performance  monitor  includes  29  additional  64-bit  event  counters, mhpmcounter3 -mhpmcounter31 . The event selector CSRs, mhpmevent3 -mhpmevent31 , are 64-bit WARL registers that control which event causes the corresponding counter to increment. The meaning of these events is defined by the platform,  but  event  0  is  defined  to  mean  "no  event."  All  counters  should  be  implemented,  but  a  legal implementation is to make both the counter and its corresponding event selector be read-only 0.

Figure 17. Hardware performance monitor counters.

<image>

The mhpmcounters are WARL registers that support up to 64 bits of precision on RV32 and RV64.

When XLEN=32, reads of the mcycle , minstret , mhpmcounter n , and mhpmevent n CSRs return bitj 31-0 of the corresponding register, and writes change only bits 31-0; reads of the mcycleh , minstreth , mhpmcounter n h , and mhpmevent n h CSRs return bits 63-32 of the corresponding register, and writes change only bits 63-32. The mhpmevent n h CSRs are provided only if the Sscofpmf extension is implemented.

## 3.1.11. Machine Counter-Enable ( mcounteren ) Register

The counter-enable mcounteren register is a 32-bit register that controls the availability of the hardware performance-monitoring counters to the next-lower privileged mode.

64

64

Figure 18. Counter-enable ( mcounteren ) register.

<image>

The settings in this register only control accessibility. The act of reading or writing this register does not affect the underlying counters, which continue to increment even when not accessible.

When the CY, TM, IR, or HPM n bit  in  the mcounteren register is clear, attempts to read the cycle , time , instret ,  or hpmcountern register  while  executing  in  S-mode  or  U-mode  will  cause  an  illegal-instruction exception.  When  one  of  these  bits  is  set,  access  to  the  corresponding  register  is  permitted  in  the  next implemented privilege mode (S-mode if implemented, otherwise U-mode).

<image>

The counter-enable bits support two common use cases with minimal hardware. For harts that do not need high-performance timers and counters, machine-mode software can trap accesses and  implement  all  features  in  software.  For  harts  that  need  high-performance  timers  and counters  but  are  not  concerned  with  obfuscating  the  underlying  hardware  counters,  the counters can be directly exposed to lower privilege modes.

In  addition,  when  the  TM  bit  in  the mcounteren register  is  clear,  attempts  to  access  the stimecmp or vstimecmp register  while  executing  in  a  mode  less  privileged  than  M  will  cause  an  illegal-instruction exception.  When  this  bit  is  set,  access  to  the stimecmp or vstimecmp register  is  permitted  in  S-mode  if implemented, and access to the vstimecmp register (via stimecmp ) is permitted in VS-mode if implemented and not otherwise prevented by the TM bit in hcounteren .

The cycle , instret ,  and hpmcountern CSRs are read-only shadows of mcycle , minstret ,  and mhpmcounter n ,  respectively. The time CSR is a read-only shadow of the memory-mapped mtime register. Analogously, when  XLEN=32,  the cycleh , instreth and hpmcounternh CSRs  are  read-only  shadows  of mcycleh , minstreth and mhpmcounternh , respectively. When XLEN=32, the timeh CSR is a read-only shadow of the upper 32 bits of the memory-mapped mtime register, while time shadows only the lower 32 bits of mtime .

<image>

Implementations can convert reads of the time and timeh CSRs into loads to the memorymapped mtime register, or emulate this functionality on behalf of less-privileged modes in Mmode software.

In harts with U-mode, the mcounteren must be implemented, but all fields are WARL and may be read-only zero,  indicating  reads  to  the  corresponding  counter  will  cause  an  illegal-instruction  exception  when executing in a less-privileged mode. In harts without U-mode, the mcounteren register should not exist.

  *Generation of a count‑overflow‑interrupt request by an hpmcounter sets the associated OF bit.*  
  *When an OF bit is set, it eventually, but not necessarily immediately, sets the LCOFIP bit in the mip / sip registers.*  
  *The LCOFIP bit is cleared by software before servicing the count overflow interrupt resulting from one or more count overflows.*

- **Delegation control**:  
  *The mideleg register controls the delegation of this interrupt to S‑mode versus M‑mode.*

- **No separate enable bit**:  
  *There are not separate overflow status and overflow interrupt enable bits.*

- **Enabling overflow interrupt generation**:  
  *In practice, enabling overflow interrupt generation (by clearing the OF bit) is done in conjunction with initializing the counter to a starting value.*

- **Re‑initialization requirement**:  
  *Once a counter has overflowed, it and the OF bit must be reinitialized before another overflow interrupt can be generated.*  
  *(Thus after mhpmcounter16 overflows, software must write a new value to mhpmcounter16 and clear mhpmevent16.OF before a subsequent overflow can produce an interrupt.)*

- **Software distinction of newly overflowed counters**:  
  *Software can distinguish newly overflowed counters (yet to be serviced by an overflow interrupt handler) from overflowed counters that have already been serviced or that are configured to not generate an interrupt on overflow, by maintaining a bit mask reflecting which counters are active and due to eventually overflow.*  
  *(A software‑maintained mask can be used to track the state of mhpmcounter16.)*

## 3.1.10. Hardware Performance Monitor

M-mode includes a basic hardware performance-monitoring facility. The mcycle CSR counts the number of clock cycles executed by the processor core on which the hart is running. The minstret CSR counts the number of instructions the hart has retired. The mcycle and minstret registers have 64-bit precision on all RV32 and RV64 harts.

The counter registers have an arbitrary value after the hart is reset, and can be written with a given value. Any CSR write takes effect after the writing instruction has otherwise completed. The mcycle CSR may be shared between harts on the same core, in which case writes to mcycle will be visible to those harts. The platform should provide a mechanism to indicate which harts share an mcycle CSR.

The  hardware  performance  monitor  includes  29  additional  64-bit  event  counters, mhpmcounter3 -mhpmcounter31 . The event selector CSRs, mhpmevent3 -mhpmevent31 , are 64-bit WARL registers that control which event causes the corresponding counter to increment. The meaning of these events is defined by the platform,  but  event  0  is  defined  to  mean  "no  event."  All  counters  should  be  implemented,  but  a  legal implementation is to make both the counter and its corresponding event selector be read-only 0.

Figure 17. Hardware performance monitor counters.

<image>

The mhpmcounters are WARL registers that support up to 64 bits of precision on RV32 and RV64.

When XLEN=32, reads of the mcycle , minstret , mhpmcounter n , and mhpmevent n CSRs return bitj 31-0 of the corresponding register, and writes change only bits 31-0; reads of the mcycleh , minstreth , mhpmcounter n h , and mhpmevent n h CSRs return bits 63-32 of the corresponding register, and writes change only bits 63-32. The mhpmevent n h CSRs are provided only if the Sscofpmf extension is implemented.
============================================================
=========

============================================================
- **mhpmcounter17 is one of the additional 64‑bit event counters** `mhpmcounter3‑mhpmcounter31`.  

- **The event selector CSR `mhpmevent17` is a 64‑bit WARL register that controls which event causes `mhpmcounter17` to increment.**  

- **Event 0 is defined to mean "no event."** (Thus selecting event 0 causes `mhpmcounter17` not to increment.)

- **All counters should be implemented, but a legal implementation is to make both the counter and its corresponding event selector be read‑only 0.** (Therefore a legal implementation may have `mhpmcounter17` read‑only returning 0 and `mhpmevent17` read‑only returning 0.)

- **The `mhpmcounters` are WARL registers that support up to 64 bits of precision on RV32 and RV64.** (Applies to `mhpmcounter17`.)

- **When XLEN=32, reads of the `mhpmcounter17` CSR return bits 31‑0 of the corresponding register, and writes change only bits 31‑0.**  

- **When XLEN=32, reads of the `mhpmcounter17h` CSR return bits 63‑32 of the corresponding register, and writes change only bits 63‑32.**  

- **Any CSR write to `mhpmcounter17` takes effect after the writing instruction has otherwise completed.**  

- **The `mhpmcounter17` register has an arbitrary value after the hart is reset, and can be written with a given value.**  

- **The `mhpmevent17h` CSRs are provided only if the `Sscofpmf` extension is implemented.** (The presence of `mhpmevent17h` determines the high‑order bits of the event selector that controls `mhpmcounter17`.)

## 3.1.11. Machine Counter-Enable ( mcounteren ) Register

The counter-enable mcounteren register is a 32-bit register that controls the availability of the hardware performance-monitoring counters to the next-lower privileged mode.

64

64

Figure 18. Counter-enable ( mcounteren ) register.

<image>

The settings in this register only control accessibility. The act of reading or writing this register does not affect the underlying counters, which continue to increment even when not accessible.

When the CY, TM, IR, or HPM n bit  in  the mcounteren register is clear, attempts to read the cycle , time , instret ,  or hpmcountern register  while  executing  in  S-mode  or  U-mode  will  cause  an  illegal-instruction exception.  When  one  of  these  bits  is  set,  access  to  the  corresponding  register  is  permitted  in  the  next implemented privilege mode (S-mode if implemented, otherwise U-mode).

<image>

The counter-enable bits support two common use cases with minimal hardware. For harts that do not need high-performance timers and counters, machine-mode software can trap accesses and  implement  all  features  in  software.  For  harts  that  need  high-performance  timers  and counters  but  are  not  concerned  with  obfuscating  the  underlying  hardware  counters,  the counters can be directly exposed to lower privilege modes.

In  addition,  when  the  TM  bit  in  the mcounteren register  is  clear,  attempts  to  access  the stimecmp or vstimecmp register  while  executing  in  a  mode  less  privileged  than  M  will  cause  an  illegal-instruction exception.  When  this  bit  is  set,  access  to  the stimecmp or vstimecmp register  is  permitted  in  S-mode  if implemented, and access to the vstimecmp register (via stimecmp ) is permitted in VS-mode if implemented and not otherwise prevented by the TM bit in hcounteren .

The cycle , instret ,  and hpmcountern CSRs are read-only shadows of mcycle , minstret ,  and mhpmcounter n ,  respectively. The time CSR is a read-only shadow of the memory-mapped mtime register. Analogously, when  XLEN=32,  the cycleh , instreth and hpmcounternh CSRs  are  read-only  shadows  of mcycleh , minstreth and mhpmcounternh , respectively. When XLEN=32, the timeh CSR is a read-only shadow of the upper 32 bits of the memory-mapped mtime register, while time shadows only the lower 32 bits of mtime .

<image>

Implementations can convert reads of the time and timeh CSRs into loads to the memorymapped mtime register, or emulate this functionality on behalf of less-privileged modes in Mmode software.

In harts with U-mode, the mcounteren must be implemented, but all fields are WARL and may be read-only zero,  indicating  reads  to  the  corresponding  counter  will  cause  an  illegal-instruction  exception  when executing in a less-privileged mode. In harts without U-mode, the mcounteren register should not exist.
============================================================
=========
RESPONSE:
=========
============================================================
- The underlying hardware performance‑monitoring counters **continue to increment even when not accessible**. (The settings in the mcounteren register only control accessibility; the act of reading or writing this register does not affect the underlying counters, which continue to increment even when not accessible.)

- The **hpmcountern CSR is a read‑only shadow of mhpmcounter n**. (The cycle, instret, and hpmcountern CSRs are read‑only shadows of mcycle, minstret, and mhpmcounter n, respectively.)  
  -> For n = 17, reading the hpmcounter17 CSR yields the current value of mhpmcounter17.

- **Access control for mhpmcounter17** is governed by the **HPM n bit (n = 17) in the mcounteren register**:  
  • *When the HPM 17 bit in the mcounteren register is clear*, attempts to read the hpmcountern register **will cause an illegal‑instruction exception** while executing in S‑mode or U‑mode.  
  • *When the HPM 17 bit in the mcounteren register is set*, access to the corresponding register **is permitted in the next implemented privilege mode** (S‑mode if implemented, otherwise U‑mode).

- In harts with U‑mode, **the HPM 17 field of mcounteren may be WARL and read‑only zero**, indicating reads to the corresponding counter **will cause an illegal‑instruction exception** when executing in a less‑privileged mode. (In harts with U‑mode, the mcounteren must be implemented, but all fields are WARL and may be read‑only zero, indicating reads to the corresponding counter will cause an illegal‑instruction exception when executing in a less‑privileged mode.)

## 3.1.12. Machine Counter-Inhibit ( mcountinhibit ) Register

Figure 19. Counter-inhibit mcountinhibit register

<image>

The counter-inhibit register mcountinhibit is a 32-bit WARL register that controls which of the hardware performance-monitoring  counters  increment.  The  settings  in  this  register  only  control  whether  the counters increment; their accessibility is not affected by the setting of this register.

When  the  CY,  IR,  or  HPM n bit  in  the mcountinhibit register  is clear,  the mcycle , minstret ,  or mhpmcountern register increments as usual. When the CY, IR, or HPM n bit is set, the corresponding counter does not increment.

The mcycle CSR may be shared between harts on the same core, in which case the mcountinhibit.CY field is also shared between those harts, and so writes to mcountinhibit.CY will be visible to those harts.

If the mcountinhibit register is not implemented, the implementation behaves as though the register were set to zero.

<image>

When  the mcycle and minstret counters  are  not  needed,  it  is  desirable  to  conditionally inhibit them to reduce energy consumption. Providing a single CSR to inhibit all counters also allows the counters to be atomically sampled.

Because the mtime counter can be shared between multiple cores, it cannot be inhibited with the mcountinhibit mechanism.
============================================================
=========
RESPONSE:
=========
============================================================
- The **mcountinhibit** CSR is a 32‑bit WARL register that controls which hardware performance‑monitoring counters increment; its settings do **not** affect the counters' accessibility.

- **When the HPM17 bit in the mcountinhibit register is clear**, the **mhpmcounter17** register **increments as usual**.

- **When the HPM17 bit in the mcountinhibit register is set**, the **mhpmcounter17** register **does not increment**.

- **If the mcountinhibit register is not implemented**, the implementation **behaves as though the register were set to zero**; therefore the HPM17 bit is considered clear and **mhpmcounter17 increments as usual**.

## 21.1. Count Overflow Control

The following bits are added to mhpmevent :

| 63   | 62   | 61   | 60   | 59    | 58    | 57   | 56   |
|------|------|------|------|-------|-------|------|------|
| OF   | MINH | SINH | UINH | VSINH | VUINH | WPRI | WPRI |

| Field   | Description                                                                  |
|---------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| OF      | Overflow status and interrupt disable bit that is set when counter overflows |
| MINH    | If set, then counting of events in M-mode is inhibited                       |
| SINH    | If set, then counting of events in S/HS-mode is inhibited                    |
| UINH    | If set, then counting of events in U-mode is inhibited                       |
| VSINH   | If set, then counting of events in VS-mode is inhibited                      |
| VUINH   | If set, then counting of events in VU-mode is inhibited                      |
| WPRI    | Reserved                                                                     |
| WPRI    | Reserved                                                                     |

For each x INH bit, if the associated privilege mode is not implemented, the bit is read-only zero.

Each of the five x INH bits, when set, inhibit counting of events while in privilege mode x .  All-zeroes for these bits results in counting of events in all modes.

The OF bit is set when the corresponding hpmcounter overflows, and remains set until written by software. Since hpmcounter  values  are  unsigned  values,  overflow is defined as unsigned  overflow  of  the implemented counter bits. Note that there is no loss of information after an overflow since the counter wraps around and keeps counting while the sticky OF bit remains set.

If supervisor mode is implemented, the 32-bit scountovf register contains read-only shadow copies of the OF bits in all 29 mhpmevent registers.

If an hpmcounter overflows while the associated OF bit is zero, then a "count overflow interrupt request" is generated.  If  the  OF  bit  is  one,  then  no  interrupt  request  is  generated.  Consequently  the  OF  bit  also functions as a count overflow interrupt disable for the associated hpmcounter.

Count  overflow  never  results  from  writes  to  the  mhpmcounter n or  mhpmevent n registers,  only  from hardware increments of counter registers.

This count-overflow-interrupt-request signal is treated as a standard local interrupt that corresponds to bit 13 in the mip / mie / sip / sie registers. The mip / sip LCOFIP and mie / sie LCOFIE bits are, respectively, the interrupt-pending and interrupt-enable bits for this interrupt. ('LCOFI' represents 'Local Count Overflow Interrupt'.)

Generation of a count-overflow-interrupt request by an hpmcounter sets the associated OF bit. When an OF bit is set, it eventually, but not necessarily immediately, sets the LCOFIP bit in the mip / sip registers. The LCOFIP bit is cleared by software before servicing the count overflow interrupt resulting from one or more count overflows. The mideleg register controls the delegation of this interrupt to S-mode versus M-mode.#

<image>

There are not separate overflow status and overflow interrupt enable bits. In practice, enabling overflow interrupt generation (by clearing the OF bit) is done in conjunction with initializing the  counter  to  a  starting  value.  Once  a  counter  has  overflowed,  it  and  the  OF  bit  must  be reinitialized before another overflow interrupt can be generated.

<image>

Software can distinguish newly overflowed counters (yet to be serviced by an overflow interrupt handler) from overflowed counters that have already been serviced or that are configured to not generate an interrupt on overflow, by maintaining a bit mask reflecting which counters are active and due to eventually overflow.

## 3.1.10. Hardware Performance Monitor

M-mode includes a basic hardware performance-monitoring facility. The mcycle CSR counts the number of clock cycles executed by the processor core on which the hart is running. The minstret CSR counts the number of instructions the hart has retired. The mcycle and minstret registers have 64-bit precision on all RV32 and RV64 harts.

The counter registers have an arbitrary value after the hart is reset, and can be written with a given value. Any CSR write takes effect after the writing instruction has otherwise completed. The mcycle CSR may be shared between harts on the same core, in which case writes to mcycle will be visible to those harts. The platform should provide a mechanism to indicate which harts share an mcycle CSR.

The  hardware  performance  monitor  includes  29  additional  64-bit  event  counters, mhpmcounter3 -mhpmcounter31 . The event selector CSRs, mhpmevent3 -mhpmevent31 , are 64-bit WARL registers that control which event causes the corresponding counter to increment. The meaning of these events is defined by the platform,  but  event  0  is  defined  to  mean  "no  event."  All  counters  should  be  implemented,  but  a  legal implementation is to make both the counter and its corresponding event selector be read-only 0.

Figure 17. Hardware performance monitor counters.

<image>

The mhpmcounters are WARL registers that support up to 64 bits of precision on RV32 and RV64.

When XLEN=32, reads of the mcycle , minstret , mhpmcounter n , and mhpmevent n CSRs return bitj 31-0 of the corresponding register, and writes change only bits 31-0; reads of the mcycleh , minstreth , mhpmcounter n h , and mhpmevent n h CSRs return bits 63-32 of the corresponding register, and writes change only bits 63-32. The mhpmevent n h CSRs are provided only if the Sscofpmf extension is implemented.

## 3.1.11. Machine Counter-Enable ( mcounteren ) Register

The counter-enable mcounteren register is a 32-bit register that controls the availability of the hardware performance-monitoring counters to the next-lower privileged mode.

64

64

Figure 18. Counter-enable ( mcounteren ) register.

<image>

The settings in this register only control accessibility. The act of reading or writing this register does not affect the underlying counters, which continue to increment even when not accessible.

When the CY, TM, IR, or HPM n bit  in  the mcounteren register is clear, attempts to read the cycle , time , instret ,  or hpmcountern register  while  executing  in  S-mode  or  U-mode  will  cause  an  illegal-instruction exception.  When  one  of  these  bits  is  set,  access  to  the  corresponding  register  is  permitted  in  the  next implemented privilege mode (S-mode if implemented, otherwise U-mode).

<image>

The counter-enable bits support two common use cases with minimal hardware. For harts that do not need high-performance timers and counters, machine-mode software can trap accesses and  implement  all  features  in  software.  For  harts  that  need  high-performance  timers  and counters  but  are  not  concerned  with  obfuscating  the  underlying  hardware  counters,  the counters can be directly exposed to lower privilege modes.

In  addition,  when  the  TM  bit  in  the mcounteren register  is  clear,  attempts  to  access  the stimecmp or vstimecmp register  while  executing  in  a  mode  less  privileged  than  M  will  cause  an  illegal-instruction exception.  When  this  bit  is  set,  access  to  the stimecmp or vstimecmp register  is  permitted  in  S-mode  if implemented, and access to the vstimecmp register (via stimecmp ) is permitted in VS-mode if implemented and not otherwise prevented by the TM bit in hcounteren .

The cycle , instret ,  and hpmcountern CSRs are read-only shadows of mcycle , minstret ,  and mhpmcounter n ,  respectively. The time CSR is a read-only shadow of the memory-mapped mtime register. Analogously, when  XLEN=32,  the cycleh , instreth and hpmcounternh CSRs  are  read-only  shadows  of mcycleh , minstreth and mhpmcounternh , respectively. When XLEN=32, the timeh CSR is a read-only shadow of the upper 32 bits of the memory-mapped mtime register, while time shadows only the lower 32 bits of mtime .

<image>

Implementations can convert reads of the time and timeh CSRs into loads to the memorymapped mtime register, or emulate this functionality on behalf of less-privileged modes in Mmode software.

In harts with U-mode, the mcounteren must be implemented, but all fields are WARL and may be read-only zero,  indicating  reads  to  the  corresponding  counter  will  cause  an  illegal-instruction  exception  when executing in a less-privileged mode. In harts without U-mode, the mcounteren register should not exist.

## 3.1.12. Machine Counter-Inhibit ( mcountinhibit ) Register

Figure 19. Counter-inhibit mcountinhibit register

<image>

The counter-inhibit register mcountinhibit is a 32-bit WARL register that controls which of the hardware performance-monitoring  counters  increment.  The  settings  in  this  register  only  control  whether  the counters increment; their accessibility is not affected by the setting of this register.

When  the  CY,  IR,  or  HPM n bit  in  the mcountinhibit register  is clear,  the mcycle , minstret ,  or mhpmcountern register increments as usual. When the CY, IR, or HPM n bit is set, the corresponding counter does not increment.

The mcycle CSR may be shared between harts on the same core, in which case the mcountinhibit.CY field is also shared between those harts, and so writes to mcountinhibit.CY will be visible to those harts.

If the mcountinhibit register is not implemented, the implementation behaves as though the register were set to zero.

<image>

When  the mcycle and minstret counters  are  not  needed,  it  is  desirable  to  conditionally inhibit them to reduce energy consumption. Providing a single CSR to inhibit all counters also allows the counters to be atomically sampled.

Because the mtime counter can be shared between multiple cores, it cannot be inhibited with the mcountinhibit mechanism.
